verified_ref: Valmiki Ramayana 5.13.47 (Southern Recension as on itihasa.io); Baroda critical edition 5.11.47. Our id 5.13.43 is off by four.
attribution_note: Hanuman speaking to himself on the city wall of Lanka is correct.
translation_note: 'Vināśe' here means self-destruction, i.e. ending one's own life (Hanuman has just weighed drowning himself or fasting to death), not 'giving up' in general. The rest of the translation is sound, though 'saṃgamaḥ' means union with good fortune or with the people he hopes for (the commentators: the wished-for meeting), not only 'meeting again'. A southern variant reads 'jīvan bhadrāṇi paśyati' ('the living see good things'). If we keep 'giving up', the reading must still say plainly that Hanuman is choosing life over suicide.
context: After searching all of Lanka through the night without finding Sita, Hanuman sits on the wall and spirals: he imagines Rama, Lakshmana, Sugriva and the whole monkey army dying of grief if he returns empty-handed, and considers drowning himself, starving to death, or living on as a forest ascetic. In this verse he turns: death brings many evils, while the living can still reach good. He then resolves to keep searching, spots the unsearched Ashoka grove, and finds Sita.

key_terms.sense: in destroying oneself there are many harms
one who stays alive reaches what is good
I will hold on to my life-breath, keep living
for the living, the hoped-for union or good fortune is assured

core_teaching: Hanuman reasons himself out of suicide: dying would bring many harms, while staying alive keeps open the possibility of good and of the reunion he is working for. The choice to live is the turning point of his search.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rāma Varmā's Tilaka
commentaries.gist: Asking whether death or life is better, Rāma Varmā says death carries all the harms Hanuman has just listed (Rama and the others would assume Sita dead and perish), whereas while Hanuman lives the desired union stays certain.
On the verse just before, Govindarāja notes that even becoming an ascetic is better than taking one's own life; Hanuman is moving away from self-destruction step by step.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Tilaka and Śiromaṇi (on 5.13.49)
commentaries.gist: Both read the next verse as unfolding the promise of 'dhruvo jīvati saṅgamaḥ': living, Hanuman can still act, even if only to bring justice against Ravana.
Renders the turn as Hanuman recognising the many ills awaiting one who takes his life, and that living he may yet succeed and bring about Rama and Sita's reunion.

practical_reading: Teachers use this as a verse of choosing life in the darkest hour: when every outcome looks ruined, staying alive keeps the door to good open, and the next step (here, one more place to search) often appears only after that choice.
misreadings: Not a general maxim about persistence at work: the verse is about not ending one's life.
Not a promise that everything lost will return; it says only that the living still have a chance at good.
Not a judgement on people who have died by suicide or on their families.
cautions: Directly about suicide: Hanuman has just considered drowning and starving himself. Any reading must name this gently and point a reader in crisis to immediate human help (a trusted person, a helpline).
Hanuman's preceding thoughts include vivid images of a whole family and army dying by suicide (5.13.20-30); do not quote that context to a vulnerable reader.
speaks_to: someone exhausted after a long search or effort with nothing to show
a person thinking 'everyone would be better off without me' or that all is lost
someone who feels they have failed people who depend on them
not_for: fresh grief after a suicide in the family (the verse argues against a choice the lost person made)
as a motivational line about career hustle, which trivialises its meaning

verified_ref: Valmiki Ramayana 5.13.48 (Southern Recension, itihasa.io); Baroda critical edition 5.11.48. Our id 5.13.44 is off by four.
translation_note: Accurate. Govindarāja's text and the critical edition read 'muhuḥ' ('again and again') for 'bahu' in the second quarter, which does not change the sense much.
context: This narrator's verse comes straight after Hanuman's resolve to stay alive (5.13.47). Even having chosen life, he still cannot see the far shore of his grief. In the next verses he gathers his courage, weighs other plans, and decides to search once more.

key_terms.sense: the far shore of grief (grief pictured as an ocean)
'elephant among monkeys', the greatest of them

core_teaching: The narrator names Hanuman's state honestly: deciding to live has not yet ended his sorrow. Grief is pictured as an ocean whose far shore he cannot yet see.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rāma Varmā's Tilaka (on 5.13.47-48)
commentaries.gist: Treats verses 47-48 together under the heading of choosing life for the sake of the hoped-for union; the sorrow in verse 48 follows directly on that choice.
Has Hanuman turning over these painful thoughts and trying not to be overwhelmed by despair before he summons his courage.

practical_reading: Useful for naming what someone feels: a decision to keep going does not make the pain go away at once, and even the strongest figure in the epic sat with grief he could not see past.
misreadings: Not a sign of weakness in Hanuman; the epic shows his greatness by letting him feel this.
Not a counsel to wallow; the next verses show him acting.
cautions: Follows directly on a passage about suicide; keep the context gentle if quoted.
speaks_to: someone who has decided to carry on but still feels heavy
grief that has no visible end yet
burnout after a failed effort
not_for: a reader looking for an action step today (pair it with 5.13.48/52 or 5.13.51/55 instead)

verified_ref: Valmiki Ramayana 5.13.51 (Southern Recension, itihasa.io); Baroda critical edition 5.11.51. Our id 5.13.47 is off by four.
attribution_note: Narrator's verse introducing Hanuman's next thoughts.
translation_note: Accurate in substance. The verse uses three words for his state (cintā, dhyāna, śoka); our 'worry and grief' compresses them. The critical edition reads 'dhyānaśokāparītātmā'.
context: Hanuman has rejected suicide and toyed with killing or kidnapping Ravana. This verse is the narrator's bridge: still not having found Sita, sunk in brooding and grief, he thinks again. What follows is the resolve to search Lanka 'again and again'.

key_terms.sense: his whole self wrapped in grief

core_teaching: A transitional verse: Hanuman's anxiety does not stop him thinking. Out of the brooding comes a clearer plan.

commentaries.gist: Explains the apparent repetition by separating three states: cintā is first deliberation, dhyāna is unbroken attention on the object, and the final verb names anxiety with no visible end.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rāma Varmā's Tilaka
commentaries.gist: Explains why Hanuman drops the plan of carrying Ravana off: the rakshasas, alarmed, might secretly kill Sita, so searching is wiser.
Describes the monkey as full of anxiety and grief at not finding Sita as he begins to plan the renewed search.

practical_reading: Anxiety and clear thinking can coexist: Hanuman thinks his way through worry rather than waiting for it to lift.
misreadings: Not an endorsement of rumination for its own sake; the brooding leads to a decision.
cautions: A narrative bridge with little content on its own; best used beside 5.13.52 (our 5.13.48).
speaks_to: someone stuck in worry who needs to think the next step through
the moment between despair and a plan
not_for: a stand-alone day's verse; it needs its neighbours to carry meaning

verified_ref: Valmiki Ramayana 5.13.52 (Southern Recension, itihasa.io); Baroda critical edition 5.11.52. Our id 5.13.48 is off by four.
translation_note: Accurate. (A southern variant reads 'hi paśyāmi'; the sense is unchanged.) Our note cites 'the resolve of 5.12.10'; we did not check that reference here.
context: Having chosen to live and rejected rash plans, Hanuman fixes on the simple task: search Lanka again and again until he sees Sita. He then reasons that bringing Rama on Sampati's word alone would be disastrous, resolves to stay in Lanka living frugally, and notices the unsearched Ashoka grove.
core_teaching: Renewed search as the practical form of not losing heart: keep looking until the goal is found.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Govindarāja's Bhūṣaṇa and Rāma Varmā's Tilaka (on 5.13.51-52)
commentaries.gist: Read the passage as Hanuman moving from bottomless anxiety to a renewed search, after setting aside the plan to seize Ravana because it could endanger Sita.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Tilaka and Bhūṣaṇa (on 5.13.53)
commentaries.gist: Both explain why he will not fetch Rama yet: if Rama came and Sita were still not found, his anger would fall on the monkeys, so finding her first is essential.
Has Hanuman vow not to stop searching Lanka on every side until he finds Rama's consort.

practical_reading: When a search or project has failed once, go back over the ground systematically rather than either quitting or escalating rashly.
misreadings: Not a call to never rest or to grind without limit; Hanuman's persistence follows a sober review of options.
Not about refusing to accept a real loss; it is about a task still within reach.
cautions: Comes just after a passage on suicide; fine for a reader who is discouraged, but avoid implying 'try harder' to someone grieving an irreversible loss.
speaks_to: job seekers or students after repeated rejections
someone searching for a solution, a diagnosis, a lost thing
anyone tempted to quit one step before the breakthrough
not_for: someone grieving a death (searching 'again and again' can feel like denial)
someone being told to persist in a harmful situation

verified_ref: Valmiki Ramayana 5.13.54 (Southern Recension, itihasa.io); Baroda critical edition 5.11.54. Our id 5.13.50 is off by four.
translation_note: Accurate. Our 'line' ('so that no one else dies because of me') is fair; the verse says 'so that all those men and monkeys do not perish on my account'.
context: Hanuman has realised that bringing Rama to Lanka before Sita is found could end in Rama's fury against the monkeys. So he decides to stay in Lanka himself, living frugally and with his senses in check, rather than return with bad news. Right after this he sees the Ashoka grove.

key_terms.sense: let them not perish because of me

core_teaching: Hanuman takes responsibility for the outcome on himself: he will endure hardship where he is rather than let others suffer from his failure.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rāma Varmā's Tilaka and Govindarāja's Bhūṣaṇa (on 5.13.53-54)
commentaries.gist: Explain that Hanuman cannot bring Rama on Sampati's testimony alone; if Sita were still missing, Rama in his anger would burn the monkeys, so Hanuman stays to finish the search himself.
Has Hanuman resolve to remain in Lanka, living abstemiously and self-controlled, so that men and monkeys do not perish through his fault.

practical_reading: Owning a task to its end: rather than passing an unfinished problem upward, stay with it and accept some personal discipline so others are not harmed by your shortfall.
misreadings: Not an instruction to fast or deprive oneself; the restraint serves the task.
Not a call to carry everyone's fate alone or to excessive guilt.
cautions: For a reader prone to over-responsibility or self-blame, 'so that no one dies because of me' can feed guilt; frame it as steady ownership, not burden.
speaks_to: a leader or caregiver holding a hard situation for others
someone deciding to stay with a difficult task rather than hand it off
not_for: a reader already crushed by guilt or self-punishing
anyone with disordered eating (the 'restricting food' wording)

verified_ref: Valmiki Ramayana 5.13.55 (Southern Recension, itihasa.io); Baroda critical edition 5.11.55. Our id 5.13.51 is off by four.
translation_note: Accurate. The critical edition reads 'abhigamiṣyāmi' for 'adhigamiṣyāmi' (no change in meaning).
context: Right after resolving to stay and search again, Hanuman notices the great Ashoka grove, the one place he has not searched. He bows to the gods, to Rama, Lakshmana and Sita, and goes there; it is where he finds Sita.

key_terms.sense: for I have not searched it yet

core_teaching: The overlooked place is where the search succeeds; renewed attention finds what despair missed.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rāma Varmā's Tilaka (on 5.13.55-57)
commentaries.gist: Calls this the turning point of the Sundara Kanda: scanning Lanka in anguish, Hanuman sees the unsearched grove, recalls Sampati's words, feels sure Sita is there, and first propitiates the gods so nothing blocks his sight of her.
Has Hanuman note the great grove of huge trees not yet searched and resolve to enter it after paying homage to the gods.

practical_reading: When you have looked everywhere, list what you have not yet tried; the answer is often in the one place skipped.
misreadings: The name 'aśoka' (sorrowless) is a pun readers often draw out; that is a devotional reading, not stated in this verse.
speaks_to: someone stuck on a problem who needs to look at the unexamined option
a renewed attempt after discouragement
not_for: someone grieving a loss that cannot be 'found' again

Our note says the tradition reads the grove as the reward of not losing heart; the Tilaka synthesis supports 'turning point' but we did not find that exact phrasing.

verified_ref: Valmiki Ramayana 5.13.58-59 (two verses; Southern Recension, itihasa.io); Baroda critical edition 5.11.58-59. Our id 5.13.54 is off by four and covers two verses.
attribution_note: Mixed speakers: the first verse (58) is the narrator, the second (59, 'namo 'stu rāmāya...') is Hanuman's own salutation. Our record lists only the narrator.
translation_note: Accurate. Govindarāja's text and the critical edition read 'candrārka' (Moon and Sun) in place of 'candrāgni' (Moon and Fire) in the last quarter; Govindarāja also reads 'mahātejā' for 'mahābāhuḥ'.
context: Having resolved to search the Ashoka grove, Hanuman stands up from his brooding and, before setting out, salutes Rama with Lakshmana, Sita, and the gods. Verse 59 ('namo 'stu rāmāya salakṣmaṇāya') is one of the best-known prayers of the Sundara Kanda and is widely recited on its own.

key_terms.sense: his senses knotted up with anxiety

core_teaching: Before a decisive act, Hanuman pauses, gathers himself and bows to Rama, Sita and the gods: effort is joined to humility and prayer.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Tilaka and Śivasahāya's Śiromaṇi (on 5.13.58)
commentaries.gist: Gloss his senses as tangled and agitated by anxiety; Śiromaṇi takes the moment's meditation as Hanuman collecting himself inwardly before rising to act.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rāma Varmā's Tilaka (on 5.13.59)
commentaries.gist: Notes that bowing to Rama, Lakshmana and Sita before the Vedic gods signals Rama's status as divine incarnation.
Cites a traditional maxim that the wise salute all the gods for Rama's cause, so that the desired outcome is secured.
Has Hanuman, after reflecting a while, rise suddenly and offer salutations to Rama with Lakshmana and the gods, then bow to Sugriva and set out mentally toward the grove.

practical_reading: Before starting something important after a stretch of anxiety, take a moment to steady yourself and offer the work to something larger than your own nerves.
misreadings: Not a magic formula that guarantees success; it accompanies Hanuman's effort rather than replacing it.
cautions: Two verses with two different speakers; split them if the app shows a single speaker.
speaks_to: the moment before an exam, interview, surgery or hard conversation
someone who wants a short prayer to begin a task
not_for: readers who want no devotional content

verified_ref: Valmiki Ramayana 5.21.15 (Southern Recension, itihasa.io); Baroda critical edition 5.19.14. Our id 5.21.14 is one off in the southern numbering (it matches the CE verse number but not the CE sarga, 19).
attribution_note: Sita to Ravana in the Ashoka grove, correct.
translation_note: Accurate. 'Ananyā rāghaveṇāham' is literally 'I am not other than (inseparable from) Raghava', as light is not separate from the sun; 'belong to' is a fair rendering. Our 'line' ('Some loyalties are not for sale') is a looser modern gloss but not wrong. The CE and a southern variant read 'prabhā yathā' (word order only).
context: Ravana has come to the Ashoka grove offering Sita wealth, queenship and power, and threatening her. Trembling, she puts a blade of grass between them and answers: she warns that Lanka will fall through his single crime and that those he has wronged will rejoice at his end. In this verse she says no wealth or power can tempt her, and in the next ones adds that having rested on Rama's arm she could not rest on another's, and urges Ravana to return her and seek Rama's friendship.

key_terms.sense: I cannot be lured or tempted
as light is with the sun

core_teaching: Sita declares that power and riches cannot buy her, because she is as inseparable from Rama as sunlight is from the sun. Her integrity is not a negotiating position but who she is.

commentaries.gist: Reads the simile theologically: Sita is Lakshmi, never separable from Vishnu born as Rama, and as sunlight adds to the sun's splendour, her presence magnifies Rama's own power.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rāma Varmā's Tilaka (on 5.21.16-17)
commentaries.gist: On the following verses, explains the image of resting on the honoured arm of the Lord, and compares Sita's exclusive bond with Rama to sacred knowledge that belongs only to a qualified, vow-completed brahmin.
Has Sita say wealth and riches cannot tempt her and that she belongs to Raghava as the sun's light cannot be parted from the sun.

practical_reading: Teachers use it for integrity under pressure: when offered money, status or comfort to betray a commitment or one's values, some things are simply not for sale.
misreadings: Not a statement that a wife has no self apart from her husband; in context it is a captive woman's defiant refusal of her abductor.
Not a rule that loyalty must be kept to someone who harms you; Sita is loyal to Rama against Ravana's coercion.
cautions: Context is sexual coercion and threat by a captor; for a reader in an abusive or coercive relationship, frame it as the right to refuse, never as 'stay loyal no matter what'.
The marital-devotion framing may land poorly for readers who are divorced, widowed or leaving a marriage.
speaks_to: someone pressured to compromise their values for money or position
a whistleblower or employee resisting a bribe
someone refusing an exploitative offer
not_for: a reader in an abusive marriage who could hear it as 'stay devoted'
someone grieving a partner (the inseparability image can sting)

verified_ref: Valmiki Ramayana 5.30.19 (Southern Recension, itihasa.io); Baroda critical edition 5.28.19. Our id 5.30.18 is one off: itihasa 5.30.18 is the verse before ('if I speak refined Sanskrit like a brahmin, Sita will take me for Ravana').
translation_note: Accurate: 'mānuṣaṃ vākyam arthavat' = human speech that carries meaning. Our 'line' ('use their language, not the one that impresses') is a fair application but stretches the verse slightly: the contrast with 'refined Sanskrit like a brahmin' is in the previous verse (5.30.18).
context: Hanuman, hidden in the tree above Sita, plans how to speak to her without terrifying her. He reasons that if he speaks refined Sanskrit like a brahmin she will remember Ravana's disguise as a mendicant and take him for Ravana (5.30.18); yet he must speak human words, or he cannot comfort her at all (this verse). He then worries she may still cry out and alert the guards, and settles on softly praising Rama from the branches.
core_teaching: To comfort a frightened person you must speak in words they can understand and trust; Hanuman chooses ordinary human speech over impressive formal language.

commentaries.gist: Takes 'human speech' to mean the vernacular of the Kosala people, because that regional speech is what Sita knows intimately and would find reassuring.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rāma Varmā's Tilaka
commentaries.gist: Says Hanuman fears that formal grammatical Sanskrit would frighten her, so he resolves to use ordinary human language, and to speak while still hidden in the foliage.
Monkey chatter would be unintelligible, so human speech is unavoidable; a brahmin's diction would recall Ravana's disguise when he abducted her.
Has Hanuman conclude that he must use the human tongue, since otherwise he cannot give the blameless lady courage.

practical_reading: When someone is frightened or grieving, speak plainly and in their own idiom; comfort depends on being understood, not on sounding learned.
misreadings: Not a dismissal of Sanskrit or learning; the point is fitting speech to the listener's fear.
Not an instruction to hide one's identity; Hanuman reveals himself as soon as she can trust him.
speaks_to: someone about to break hard news or comfort a frightened person
parents, carers, doctors, teachers explaining to someone anxious
a person who over-prepares and over-formalises when someone needs warmth
not_for: a reader wanting comfort for themselves today (this is guidance for the comforter)
research_note: Numbering: our 30.18 = itihasa/CE 19. The verse our note paraphrases ('polished Sanskrit would make Sita take him for Ravana') is the preceding verse 5.30.18.

verified_ref: Valmiki Ramayana 5.30.35 (Southern Recension, itihasa.io); Baroda critical edition 5.28.35. Our id is one off.
translation_note: Accurate. 'Asatyāni yuddhāni' = battles are unreliable (victory never guaranteed); 'saṃśayo me na rocate' = I don't like taking a risk.
context: Hanuman has found Sita and is considering what to do if she cries out and the guards attack. He knows he could kill thousands of rakshasas, but if he were killed or captured no one else could leap the ocean and Rama's mission would fail. So he refuses to turn a mission already as good as achieved into a gamble, and plans to approach Sita quietly.

key_terms.sense: battles are uncertain, their outcome unreliable
a gamble does not please me
a task whose success is already sure

core_teaching: A prudent agent does not risk a nearly-secured result for a fight whose outcome is uncertain; secure the essential task first.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rāma Varmā's Tilaka
commentaries.gist: Reads 'asatyāni' as battles whose victory is never certain; no prudent envoy would endanger a mission already settled in its outcome.
Whoever exposes a sure undertaking to needless battle-risk becomes the destroyer of his master's cause, foolish and deserving blame.
Battles now are 'unreliable' because they would put Sita's very life at risk.
Has Hanuman say battles are hazardous and he dislikes so uncertain an enterprise; a wise person takes no needless risk.

practical_reading: Before a dramatic move, ask whether it risks what you have already nearly secured; finish the certain part first, then take on the uncertain one.
misreadings: Not a rule against all risk or courage; Hanuman fights later, once the essential task is done.
Not cowardice: he is sure he could win, but will not stake the mission on it.
speaks_to: someone tempted by a confrontation that could derail a near-finished goal
founders, managers, students near the finish line
anger that wants a showdown
not_for: someone paralysed by fear of any risk, who needs encouragement to act

verified_ref: Valmiki Ramayana 5.30.42-43 (two verses; Southern Recension, itihasa.io); Baroda critical edition 5.28.42-43. Our id 5.30.40 is two off; itihasa 5.30.40 is the line 'How may she hear me and not be alarmed? Thus thinking, wise Hanuman made up his mind'.
translation_note: Minor: the Sanskrit says he will deliver Rama's own auspicious, dharma-filled words ('vacanāni' of Rama, 'samarpayan' = handing over), not 'good and true words about Ram'. In the narrative he in fact recites Rama's story (5.31), and the prior verse speaks of praising Rama, so 'about Ram' is defensible as the gist, but the verse's own wording is 'Rama's words'. 'Samādadhe' = I will arrange everything (or, Śiromaṇi: answer all her doubts) so she believes.
context: Having weighed the dangers of speaking openly, Hanuman decides to stay hidden in the branches and begin by extolling Rama, the one Sita's whole mind is fixed on, so she is not startled. In these two verses he resolves to deliver Rama's good words in a sweet voice and arrange everything so she can believe him. The next sarga is his gentle recital of Rama's story.

key_terms.sense: I will arrange it all, set everything right

core_teaching: Hanuman plans to win a terrified listener's trust by starting gently with what she loves most (Rama) and speaking sweetly, rather than by asserting himself.

commentaries.gist: Without showing his monkey form, Hanuman will keep Sita calm purely by singing Rama's praises.
Glosses 'samādadhe' as answering every doubt Sita might raise, and notes Hanuman speaks from inside the tree's boughs.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rāma Varmā's Tilaka
commentaries.gist: Takes 'samādadhe' in a future sense, 'I shall speak it all properly', and reads the preceding verse's compound as Sita whose mind is fixed on Rama.
Has Hanuman resolve to speak gently of Rama, praising his piety and renown in sweet tones, and do everything to win her confidence.

practical_reading: To earn the trust of someone frightened or suspicious, begin gently with what matters to them and speak softly; trust is built before your own agenda.
misreadings: Not manipulation or flattery: Hanuman speaks truthfully ('avitatham' in 5.30.44) and only to relieve her fear.
cautions: Two verses merged under one id.
speaks_to: someone approaching an estranged or frightened person
a new caregiver, teacher or counsellor building trust
reaching out after a rupture
not_for: a reader wanting personal consolation (this is about how to approach another)

verified_ref: Valmiki Ramayana 5.34.6 (Southern Recension, itihasa.io); Baroda critical edition 5.32.6. Our id is one off: itihasa 5.34.5 is the narrator's line introducing her words.
translation_note: Accurate. 'Kalyāṇī ... gāthā laukikī' = an auspicious popular saying; 'eti jīvantam ānando naraṃ varṣaśatād api' = joy comes to the living person even after a hundred years. The CE reads 'me' for 'mā'.
context: Hanuman has just told Sita that Rama is well and asks after her, and that Lakshmana bows to her. Thrilled in every limb, Sita, who the night before had resolved to end her life, quotes a folk proverb: joy comes to one who stays alive, even after a hundred years. A moment later her suspicion that he is Ravana in disguise returns, and Hanuman has to win her trust again.

key_terms.sense: joy comes to the one who is alive

core_teaching: Sita recognises the truth of a folk saying: as long as one stays alive, joy can still come, however long the wait. The commentators draw the moral that one should bear great sorrow and keep living.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rāma Varmā's Tilaka and Govindarāja's Bhūṣaṇa
commentaries.gist: Because Sita kept her life through unbearable grief and has now heard unhoped-for news of Rama, she praises the popular saying as true; their gloss draws the lesson that one should endure even great sorrow and go on living.
The joy at this meeting is mutual: Hanuman rejoices at having found the queen, Sita at seeing Rama's messenger.
Has Sita, trembling with delight at news of the two brothers, say the wise hold that happiness comes to a man even after a hundred years.

practical_reading: A verse of hope for long waits: staying alive through a dark stretch keeps open the chance that good news, reunion or joy will still come.
misreadings: Not a promise of a specific outcome or timeline.
Not a reason to dismiss present pain ('it will be fine eventually'); Sita had suffered for months and nearly died.
cautions: Sita had decided to hang herself the night before (5.28); suitable as a protective line for someone in despair, but any reading should also point a reader in crisis to immediate help.
The joy here is reunion with a living person; for fresh bereavement it can sound like a hollow promise.
speaks_to: someone in a long, dark wait (illness, separation, unemployment, legal limbo)
a reader who has thought of giving up on life
people separated from loved ones
not_for: fresh grief over a death, where 'joy will come' can feel dismissive
research_note: Our note says Bharata repeats this saying when Rama returns; this is widely reported (Yuddha Kanda, Bharata's meeting with Hanuman) but we did not verify it here.

verified_ref: Valmiki Ramayana 5.36.47 (Southern Recension, itihasa.io); Baroda critical edition 5.34.45. Our id 5.36.44 is three off; itihasa 5.36.44 is Hanuman's line that Rama is always sleepless and wakes saying 'Sita'.
attribution_note: Narrator's verse; our listener field is empty (should be 'the reader').
translation_note: Accurate in substance. 'Ambudaśeṣacandrā' = with its moon (partly) veiled by the last clouds; our 'the moon rising through the last of the rain clouds' is a fair image. The southern variant 'śaranmukhe sāmbudaśeṣacandrā' does not change the sense.
context: Hanuman has given Sita Rama's ring and describes Rama's state: he barely sleeps, wakes calling her name, sighs at every flower, and strives only to win her back. Sita's sorrow lifts at hearing Rama praised, yet she grieves at hearing of his grief. Valmiki pictures her as an early-autumn night whose moon is still partly veiled by the last clouds.

key_terms.sense: her sorrow gone through hearing Rama extolled
grieving equally because of Rama's grief
a night at the start of autumn
with its moon among the remaining clouds

core_teaching: Valmiki's image for mixed feeling: relief and sorrow can be present at once, like a moon half clear, half veiled.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rāma Varmā's Tilaka
commentaries.gist: Sita is freed from the sorrow born of doubt by hearing of Rama's sleepless love, yet struck with an equal sorrow on hearing of his torment.
Admires the simile: like an autumn night with its moon partly clear and partly clouded, Sita is both brightened and shadowed.
Rama's sleeplessness and murmuring of Sita's name show the steadfast love of the best of men in separation.
Sita is delighted by Rama's praises but grieved to hear of his pain, like the autumn moon passing into a dark cloud and reappearing.

practical_reading: Gives permission to feel two things at once: good news about someone you love can bring relief and fresh pain together.
misreadings: Not a demand to resolve the feeling into one; the verse simply describes both.
speaks_to: mixed feelings at news from a distant or suffering loved one
long-distance relationships, families separated by migration, hospital or prison
bittersweet moments of hope
not_for: someone needing a clear action step

verified_ref: Valmiki Ramayana 5.39.21 (Southern Recension, itihasa.io); Baroda critical edition 5.37.20. Our id is one off; itihasa 5.39.20 is her request to stay a day and leave tomorrow.
translation_note: Accurate. 'Muhūrtaṃ mokṣaṇam' = release for a short while. The CE reads 'mama ced alpabhāgyāyāḥ ... vīryavan' (minor). Note the vocative is 'vānara' (monkey), not 'friend'; 'friend' is our warm rendering.
context: Hanuman is about to leave Lanka with Sita's token. Gazing at him again and again, she asks him to stay one more day hidden somewhere and leave tomorrow: his nearness would give her a moment's release from her great sorrow, and once he goes she fears for her very life until he returns and doubts how the army will cross the sea. Hanuman reassures her and then departs.

key_terms.sense: from your presence, your being near

core_teaching: A frightened, lonely person asks for presence: simply having a friend near brings a moment's relief from sorrow.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Tilaka and Śiromaṇi (on 5.39.22)
commentaries.gist: On the next verse, once Hanuman leaves, uncertainty about his return leaves her life itself in doubt; Śiromaṇi reads it as a rhetorical question.
Has Sita ask him to tarry one day in a hidden spot, saying his presence will let her forget her misfortune for a while.

practical_reading: Presence itself heals: sometimes what helps most is staying a little longer with someone who is struggling, even without solving anything.
misreadings: Not a sign that Sita is weak; she has endured months of captivity.
cautions: The next verse speaks of doubt about her survival; keep context gentle.
speaks_to: loneliness, especially during illness or isolation
someone saying goodbye to a visitor, child, or friend
the comforter wondering whether just being there matters
not_for: someone who needs to be told to let go of a relationship
research_note: No classical comment on this exact verse in the itihasa synthesis; commentaries cited are on the adjacent verse.

verified_ref: Valmiki Ramayana 5.39.44 (Southern Recension, itihasa.io); Baroda critical edition 5.37.43. Our id is four off.
translation_note: Accurate. 'Kālakāṅkṣiṇī' = one who waits expectantly for the time; Tilaka and Govindarāja gloss it as counting the remaining days.
context: At parting, Hanuman promises Sita that Rama and Lakshmana will soon come on his back with a vast army, destroy Lanka, kill Ravana and take her home. This verse is his summary: take heart, wait for the time, and you will soon see Rama blazing like fire. He then adds that she will be reunited with Rama like Rohini with the moon, and see the far shore of her grief.

key_terms.sense: waiting for the right time (counting the days)

core_teaching: Hanuman asks Sita to take heart and wait for the appointed time, because help is truly on its way; waiting is asked of her only because others are acting.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rāma Varmā's Tilaka and Govindarāja's Bhūṣaṇa
commentaries.gist: Both gloss 'kālakāṅkṣiṇī' as being intent on counting the days remaining until Rama arrives.
Because she will soon see Rama, she should be expectant and take comfort; the next verse's reunion like Rohini with the moon means she will attain union with Rama.
Hanuman's parting reassurance to Sita that Rama will soon come and free her (chapter read for context).

practical_reading: When help is genuinely on its way, the task is to steady yourself and count the days rather than despair; Hanuman's own action stands behind the promise.
misreadings: Not a call to passive waiting where no help is coming.
Not a timeline promise.
cautions: Its promise of rescue and violence against the captor ('Ravana slain') is part of the context; keep focus on 'take heart'.
speaks_to: waiting for test results, a visa, a release, a reunion
someone in a hard place who knows help is coming
families awaiting a loved one's return
not_for: someone whose situation has no rescue coming (can feel like false hope)

verified_ref: Valmiki Ramayana 5.41.6 (Southern Recension, itihasa.io); Baroda critical edition 5.39.6. Reference correct.
translation_note: Accurate: no single means accomplishes even a small task; one who knows a goal in many ways can achieve it.
context: Having comforted Sita and taken her token, Hanuman decides his mission is not complete until he has also gauged the enemy's strength. He dismisses conciliation, gifts and division as useless with the rakshasas and settles on force. The verse before says a good envoy accomplishes extra tasks without harming the main one; this verse adds that one must know many ways to a goal. He then smashes the Ashoka grove to provoke a fight, which leads to his capture and the burning of Lanka.

key_terms.sense: knows the goal (and its means) in many ways

core_teaching: Effective agents are resourceful: they understand a goal from several angles and do not depend on one method.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rāma Varmā's Tilaka and Govindarāja's Bhūṣaṇa (on 5.41.5-6)
commentaries.gist: Both defend an envoy accomplishing further useful tasks for his master, provided they do not undercut the original mission; Tilaka calls this an ornament of a good messenger.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Tilaka and Bhūṣaṇa (on 5.41.7)
commentaries.gist: Hanuman wants to learn the relative strength of the enemy before returning so his master's command is fully done; otherwise he could not answer if asked about Ravana's army.
Has Hanuman set aside negotiation, gifts and dissension as useless here and choose valour, noting that a skilful messenger achieves his main aim and others besides.

practical_reading: Don't rely on a single plan; understand a goal well enough to have several routes to it, and add value beyond the brief without endangering the core task.
misreadings: Not an endorsement of using force; in context Hanuman's 'many ways' leads to provoking a fight, and later he regrets the anger that followed.
Not 'do everything at once'; the preceding verse insists extra tasks must not harm the main one.
cautions: Belongs to the run-up to the burning of Lanka; pair with 5.55.3-10 if using the arc.
speaks_to: professionals and students stuck on one approach
project leads planning contingencies
not_for: someone already overwhelmed who needs to simplify

verified_ref: Valmiki Ramayana 5.55.3 (Southern Recension, itihasa.io); Baroda critical edition 5.53.3. Reference correct.
attribution_note: Hanuman to himself after burning Lanka, correct.
translation_note: Accurate. Govindarāja and the CE read 'dhanyās te puruṣaśreṣṭhāḥ' for the first 'mahātmānaḥ' (the vulgate repeats 'mahātmānaḥ').
context: Hanuman, captured and with his tail set on fire, has burned much of Lanka. Looking at the blazing, terrified city, he is seized by dread that Sita may have died in the fire, and turns on himself. This verse opens a series of reflections on anger: blessed are those who quench rising anger with wisdom. He curses himself, considers ending his life, then reasons that Sita's own power must have protected her, hears from celestial beings that she is safe, and goes to see her again.

key_terms.sense: as water quenches a blazing fire

core_teaching: Hanuman, realising what his anger may have cost, praises those who use understanding to stop anger as it rises, the way water puts out fire.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rāma Varmā's Tilaka
commentaries.gist: Hanuman concludes that anger was the root of his reprehensible act; the repetition of 'mahātmānaḥ' is no flaw, as it comes from his overwhelming distress.
Glosses the 'great souls' as people of supreme self-discipline, and notes Govindarāja's reading 'best of men'.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Tilaka and Śiromaṇi (on 5.55.1-2)
commentaries.gist: Having put out his tail in the sea, Hanuman sees the city's ruin and fears Janaki herself has burned; dread and self-condemnation rise in him.
Has Hanuman reflect that he has done something reprehensible and that blessed are the great souls who extinguish anger born in them as water quenches fire.

practical_reading: Notice anger at the moment it rises and use judgement to put it out before it acts; even heroes learn this after the damage.
misreadings: Not a teaching that anger is never felt by good people; Hanuman, the ideal devotee, felt it.
Not a call to suppress justified grievance; it is about stopping anger from acting blindly.
cautions: Followed by intense self-condemnation and thoughts of ending his life (5.55.7-13); a reader prone to shame should get the arc's resolution (Sita is safe) too.
speaks_to: someone who has just lost their temper and regrets it
parents, partners, managers working on reactivity
after an outburst at work or home
not_for: someone whose anger is a response to abuse they are suffering (it can sound like 'you should calm down')

verified_ref: Valmiki Ramayana 5.55.5 (Southern Recension, itihasa.io). Not in the Baroda critical edition: 5.55.4-7 are southern additions (starred in the CE).
translation_note: Accurate: the furious person never knows what may and may not be said; for the angry there is no deed undone and no word unsaid.
context: Part of Hanuman's reflection on anger after burning Lanka, just after praising those who quench rising anger. The verse before says an angry man will commit any sin, even kill his teachers and insult the good; the one after says he is truly a man who sheds anger by forbearance as a snake sheds its old skin. He then curses himself for having forgotten Sita.

key_terms.sense: what should and should not be said
there is nothing he will not do
there is nothing he will not say

core_teaching: Anger destroys discrimination: in rage a person loses the sense of what must not be said or done.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rāma Varmā's Tilaka (on 5.55.4-6)
commentaries.gist: Reads verses 4-6 as a list of anger's faults: for the angry, any harmful act conceived by a warped mind becomes possible; the passage closes with the snake shedding its skin as the image of forbearance.
Govindarāja's text of the preceding verse reads it as 'who, when angry, would not commit sin?'; Tilaka explains there is no moment when an angry man refrains.
Has Hanuman say the one who gives way to wrath cannot tell when to speak and when to be silent, and no wrong is beyond him.

practical_reading: In a heated moment, assume your judgement about what to say is compromised; pause before speaking or sending.
misreadings: Not a claim that angry people are evil; it describes what anger does to anyone.
cautions: Southern-only verse (not in the critical edition); fine for the app but note it if citing CE numbering.
speaks_to: regret after harsh words to a partner, child, parent or colleague
someone about to send an angry message
family conflicts
not_for: a victim of someone else's rage, who may hear it as excusing the abuser

verified_ref: Valmiki Ramayana 5.55.10-11 (two verses; Southern Recension, itihasa.io); Baroda critical edition 5.53.6-7. Our id covers two verses.
translation_note: Our translation follows Tilaka and Śiromaṇi ('this', i.e. burning Lanka, was a trifling act, yet it destroyed the root of Rama's mission). Govindarāja reads 'this task' as the main mission, already almost complete with only the report remaining; both are traditional readings. Our 'line' ('I won a small fight') adds an idea not in the verse: no fight is mentioned; better 'I did a small thing in anger and wrecked what I came for'.
context: Looking at the burning city, Hanuman fears Sita has died in the fire. He calls himself an arsonist who forgot Sita and betrayed his master, and here concludes that in anger he has cut the root of the mission; since no part of Lanka seems unburnt, she must have perished. He considers throwing himself into fire or the sea, but then reasons that Sita's virtue protects her, notes that his own tail did not burn, hears celestial beings say she is safe, and goes to see her before leaving.

key_terms.sense: a small, trivial act (or: a task nearly done)

core_teaching: Hanuman sees that a moment's anger can undo the very purpose one has worked for. His fear proves mistaken, but the lesson about anger stands.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rāma Varmā's Tilaka and Śivasahāya's Śiromaṇi
commentaries.gist: Take 'this task' as the burning of Lanka, done as an effortless trifle, which destroyed the root of Rama's main purpose.
Takes 'this task' as the great mission of finding Sita, nearly finished with only the report to Rama left, now ruined at its root.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of the three commentators (on 5.55.11-12)
commentaries.gist: Because no spot is seen unburnt, Hanuman infers Sita's death; Śiromaṇi calls it perversity of judgement, and Govindarāja explains the next verse as resolving to give up his life at once.
Has Hanuman reproach himself as a shameless wrongdoer who, forgetting Sita, has slain his lord by fire.

practical_reading: Before acting in anger, ask what you came to do; the cost of a small outburst can be the thing you care about most.
misreadings: Not proof that Sita died: Hanuman's fear is mistaken, and the sarga resolves it.
Not a counsel to self-punishment; Hanuman's despair passes once he thinks clearly.
cautions: Immediately followed by Hanuman resolving to end his life (5.55.12-13); never quote that part to a reader in distress, and always give the resolution.
Two verses merged.
speaks_to: regret after an outburst that harmed a relationship or project
someone who sabotaged a near-finished effort through impulse
not_for: someone consumed by guilt or shame already
a reader with suicidal thoughts (context)

verified_ref: Valmiki Ramayana 6.1.12 (Southern Recension, itihasa.io); Baroda critical edition 6.1.11. Reference correct.
attribution_note: Rama speaking about Hanuman in the presence of Hanuman and Sugriva; correct.
translation_note: Accurate. 'Dīnasya' = of me who am in a poor or wretched state; 'priyākhyātuḥ' = of the one who told me good news. Our 'line' adds 'So I'll give what I have: a hug', which is the next verse (6.1.13), not this one.
context: Hanuman has returned with Sita's jewel and message. Rama praises his feat as unmatched and says that by finding Sita, Hanuman has saved Rama, Lakshmana and the whole Raghu line. Then a pang: in exile he has nothing fitting to give in return. In the next verse he gives his embrace as his 'all', and holds Hanuman close.

key_terms.sense: it torments my mind all the more
of the bringer of good news

core_teaching: Rama's gratitude is so great that being unable to repay it pains him; the next verse shows that the gift of oneself is the fitting return.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rāma Varmā's Tilaka
commentaries.gist: The distress of being unable to repay at once overshadows even his joy at news of Sita.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Govindarāja's Bhūṣaṇa and Śiromaṇi
commentaries.gist: Both read 'prakarṣati' as violently agitating or tormenting the mind, and gloss the old verb 'kurmi' as 'I do'.
Explains why an embrace is called Rama's 'all': the Lord's very being is bliss, so his embrace bestows that bliss.
Has Rama, full of joy, praise Hanuman's mission as the most arduous in the world, beyond anyone else (chapter read for context).

practical_reading: Gratitude that cannot be repaid in kind can still be expressed fully, with presence and affection; the wish to repay is itself part of a grateful heart.
misreadings: Not a statement that love must always be repaid; Rama's pain is gratitude, not debt-anxiety.
speaks_to: someone who has received great help and feels unable to repay it
people in hard times who cannot give material gifts
not_for: someone burdened by feeling permanently indebted (could reinforce guilt)

verified_ref: Valmiki Ramayana 6.10.25 (Southern Recension, itihasa.io; a three-line verse). Not in the Baroda critical edition (6.10.22-29 are southern additions). Our id 6.10.17 is eight off.
translation_note: Accurate. Southern variants read 'śrāvaṇe' ('in making this counsel heard') and 'saṃvidhāya' for 'sampradhārya'. SETTING ERROR: our setting says Vibhishana goes to Ravana 'privately', and our note says 'counsel given privately'. The narrator's next verse says he spoke 'in the midst of [Ravana's] own ministers', and Shastri likewise has him speak in the presence of the ministers. He did go to Ravana's palace on his own initiative, but the counsel was not private.
context: Disturbed by the omens in Lanka since Sita's arrival, Vibhishana goes to Ravana's palace in the morning and, before his ministers, urges that Sita be returned as the only remedy, asking not to be blamed if he speaks out of misjudgement or attachment to life. In this verse he explains why he alone speaks: the ministers have shrunk from saying it, but what he has seen and heard must be told; Ravana should weigh it and act. Ravana, feverish with infatuation, rejects him.

key_terms.sense: all the ministers have held back
it must be said by me
what has been seen or heard
weighing it properly, as is right

core_teaching: When those around a leader stay silent out of fear, a loyal advisor must still report what he has seen and heard, and leave the decision to the leader.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rāma Varmā's Tilaka
commentaries.gist: Explains why Vibhishana speaks when senior counsellors like Prahasta are present: they withdrew out of fear of Ravana, which exposes the cowardice of men who think themselves warriors; his brotherly bond compels him.
The narrator calls the advice fit for all three times: it redeems the past by expiating the abduction, helps the present, and protects the future by keeping dharma.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Tilaka and Bhūṣaṇa (on 6.10.23-24)
commentaries.gist: Vibhishana pre-empts the king's anger: even if he errs from misunderstanding or love of life, the omens threaten everyone in Lanka.
Has Vibhishana, in the presence of the ministers alone, say they dare not counsel the king out of fear, but he feels bound to report what he has seen and heard.

practical_reading: When colleagues or family go quiet out of fear, someone must still name the problem respectfully and leave the decision with the person responsible.
misreadings: Not licence to lecture or to publicly humiliate; Vibhishana speaks gently and asks to be forgiven.
Not a guarantee that speaking up will be welcomed; he is rejected.
cautions: Southern-only verse; note if CE numbering is used.
speaks_to: employees or family members who see a problem everyone is avoiding
whistleblowers weighing whether to speak
not_for: someone in a dangerous situation where speaking up could put them at risk without support
research_note: Setting/note say 'privately'; the text says in the presence of the ministers. Please correct.

verified_ref: Valmiki Ramayana 6.16.21 (Southern Recension, itihasa.io); Baroda critical edition 6.10.16. Our id 6.16.20 is one off (itihasa 6.16.20: the undisciplined, under Time's sway, do not accept sound advice).
attribution_note: Vibhishana to Ravana, correct. As our note says, Rāma Varmā confirms Vibhishana is repeating Maricha's earlier maxim (Aranya Kanda).
translation_note: Accurate. 'Pathya' = wholesome, good for you (like a medical diet); 'apriya' = unwelcome.
context: After Ravana insults Vibhishana as a traitor in open court, Vibhishana rises into the air with four companions and answers. Elder brothers deserve respect, he says, but he cannot bear such words; people under Time's sway reject good advice. This verse is his famous maxim. He adds that he cannot watch his brother perish like a burning house, asks forgiveness, wishes him well and leaves for Rama's camp.

key_terms.sense: people who say pleasing things are easy to find
of what is unwelcome but beneficial
both the speaker and the listener are rare

core_teaching: Flatterers are always available; honest, beneficial counsel is rare, and so is the person willing to hear it.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rāma Varmā's Tilaka
commentaries.gist: Notes Vibhishana is recalling Maricha's well-known maxim; men of unsteady mind, caught by Time, reject sound policy, while speakers and hearers of unwelcome good counsel are rare.
Vibhishana explains that he spoke because he could not passively watch his brother perish, like a house on fire.
Has Vibhishana say flatterers are easy to find, but rare are those who speak salutary though unpleasing words, or those who listen to them.

practical_reading: Value the people who tell you hard truths, and practise being a listener who can hear them; check whether you surround yourself with agreement.
misreadings: Not licence to be harsh and call it honesty; the counsel must be 'pathya' (genuinely for the other's good).
Not a reason to dismiss all kind words as flattery.
speaks_to: leaders and managers
someone whose honest advice was rejected
families where one member keeps raising a hard truth
not_for: a reader being criticised harshly by someone who claims to be 'just honest'

verified_ref: Valmiki Ramayana 6.16.25 (Southern Recension, itihasa.io; three-line verse); Baroda critical edition 6.10.20 (lines 2-3 only; the line asking forgiveness is a southern addition). Our id is one off (itihasa 6.16.24: even mighty warriors overtaken by Time crumble like sand dams).
translation_note: Accurate. Note that the first line ('forgive what I said...out of respect for you as my elder') is not in the critical edition. Rāma Varmā reads 'be happy without me' as carrying irony: happy now, without my unwelcome counsel.
context: These are Vibhishana's parting words after Ravana publicly calls him a traitor. Having warned that even great warriors crumble like dams of sand when their time comes, he asks forgiveness for words spoken for his elder's good, urges Ravana to protect himself and the city, wishes him well and leaves. The narrator adds that at their end men do not accept friends' good counsel. Vibhishana then flies to Rama's camp to seek refuge.

key_terms.sense: wishing your good, because you are my elder
may it go well with you

core_teaching: Having done his duty of honest counsel, Vibhishana leaves without hatred: he asks pardon, wishes his brother well, and goes.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rāma Varmā's Tilaka
commentaries.gist: Vibhishana asks pardon for hard truth spoken out of duty to an elder and bids Ravana guard himself and Lanka; 'be happy without me' carries irony: free now of my unwelcome advice.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Tilaka, Śiromaṇi and Bhūṣaṇa (on 6.16.24)
commentaries.gist: Answering Ravana's pride, all three say even valiant, well-armed warriors, once seized by death through unrighteousness, collapse like dams of sand.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Śiromaṇi and Bhūṣaṇa (on 6.16.26)
commentaries.gist: Men whose lifespan is spent spurn their friends' salutary words at the hour of death.
Vibhishana's farewell to Ravana after being insulted (chapter read for context).

practical_reading: You can leave a relationship or workplace that refuses honest counsel without bitterness: say your piece, wish them well, protect yourself, and go.
misreadings: Not a model for walking out at the first disagreement; Vibhishana leaves after repeated counsel and public humiliation.
Not betrayal: the text presents his departure as dharmic.
cautions: Leaving family can be painful; a reader estranged from a sibling or parent may find it validating or raw. Frame with care.
speaks_to: someone leaving a family, team or community after being rejected for honesty
estrangement handled without hatred
not_for: someone being urged to cut off family they want to reconcile with

verified_ref: Valmiki Ramayana 6.17.52 (Southern Recension, itihasa.io); Baroda critical edition 6.11.43. Our id is two off (itihasa 6.17.50 is the narrator introducing Hanuman's smooth, meaningful, sweet and concise speech).
attribution_note: Hanuman to Rama in council, correct.
translation_note: Accurate in substance. 'Gauravāt' is read by Govindarāja as 'because of the honour you do me in consulting me', which fits our 'out of respect for you'; others take it as 'because of the matter's weight'. 'Yathārtham' = truthfully, as the matter really is.
context: Vibhishana has arrived asking for refuge, and Rama asks his allies whether to accept him. Sugriva, Angada, Sharabha, Jambavan and Mainda counsel suspicion, testing or delay. Hanuman speaks last, prefacing his view with this verse, then points out flaws in their proposals (one cannot test a person without employing him, yet employing him rashly is risky) and argues from Vibhishana's demeanour that he is sincere.

key_terms.sense: out of respect (or because the matter is weighty)

core_teaching: Hanuman models how to give counsel: not to win an argument, compete with colleagues, show off or push a personal wish, but honestly and out of respect.

commentaries.gist: Contrasts four bad motives (debating skill, ministerial rivalry, conceit, caprice) with 'gauravāt', which he reads as the honour Rama shows by consulting him.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rāma Varmā's Tilaka
commentaries.gist: Hanuman tactfully passes over Sugriva's rash demand for execution and answers the others' testing proposals in turn, arguing for immediate acceptance; his speech is measured in words.
Describes Hanuman as steeped in learning and his speech as free of blemishes; on 6.17.54, one cannot gauge ability without a task, yet a hasty appointment risks ruin.
Introduces Hanuman, foremost of those versed in the scriptures, speaking in sweet accents and words of integrity.

practical_reading: Before offering an opinion in a meeting or family discussion, check your motive: am I trying to win, outshine someone, or get my way, or am I helping the decision?
misreadings: Not false modesty: Hanuman goes on to disagree firmly with the others.
speaks_to: anyone giving feedback or advice
team members in a heated discussion
people who feel compelled to win arguments
not_for: a reader needing comfort rather than guidance

verified_ref: Valmiki Ramayana 6.18.3 (Southern Recension, itihasa.io); Baroda critical edition 6.12.3. Reference correct.
translation_note: Accurate. 'Satām etad agarhitam' = this is not blamed by the good. Our note on the Śrīvaiṣṇava reading is supported: Govindarāja glosses 'mitrabhāva' as the stance of one who has taken refuge.
context: After hearing his allies' doubts and Hanuman's argument that Vibhishana is sincere, Rama gives his own view: he will never abandon one who comes in friendship, even if he has faults. Sugriva objects again that a man who deserts his own brother in calamity may desert anyone. Rama then argues that Vibhishana cannot harm him, tells the story of the dove, cites the sage Kandu, and makes his vow of refuge.

key_terms.sense: one who has come in friendship
even if he has a fault
the good do not blame this

core_teaching: Rama will not turn away someone who comes to him in friendship, even if that person is flawed; the righteous see no fault in accepting him.

commentaries.gist: Reads 'mitrabhāva' as the attitude of one taking refuge, even if only outwardly feigned, and cites a Vedic rule that one who has surrendered is never handed back even if deserving death.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rāma Varmā's Tilaka
commentaries.gist: Where Hanuman argued Vibhishana was innocent, Rama goes further and concedes he may have faults, to establish that acceptance of a supplicant is unconditional.
Takes 'friendship' as standing for the attitude of a friend or servant; on Sugriva's reply, he notes Sugriva thinks debating Vibhishana's guilt is pointless since he abandoned his brother.
Has Rama say he will never refuse one who presents himself as a friend, and that even if mistaken, no honest man could reproach him.

practical_reading: Make room for people who come to you in good faith even if they carry faults or a bad history; acceptance need not wait for perfection.
misreadings: Not a demand that victims welcome back those who harmed them; Rama is the powerful party, and the refugee has done him no wrong.
Not naivety: Rama has heard and weighed every objection.
cautions: For readers who have been hurt, 'never turn away anyone' can feel like pressure to tolerate harmful people; keep the protector framing.
speaks_to: someone deciding whether to give a newcomer, a reformed person or an outsider a chance
teams and communities welcoming people with a past
a reader who fears they are too flawed to be accepted
not_for: someone being pressured to reconcile with an abuser

verified_ref: Valmiki Ramayana 6.18.25 (Southern Recension, itihasa.io); Baroda critical edition 6.12.12. Our id 6.18.23 is two off (itihasa 6.18.23 is Rama saying he could slay all demons with a fingertip).
translation_note: Accurate. The previous verse (6.18.24) adds that the dove honoured the hunter and even offered him its own flesh.
context: Sugriva still fears Vibhishana is a spy. Rama first says no rakshasa could harm him even if he wanted to, then recalls a tale of a dove that welcomed and even offered its own flesh to the hunter who had caught its mate and came to it for shelter. If a bird could do that, how much more should he. He then quotes the sage Kandu on protecting refugees and makes his vow.

key_terms.sense: the one who carried off its mate
how much more a person like me

core_teaching: An argument from the lesser to the greater: if even a bird sheltered the one who wronged it when he came for refuge, a person of dharma must do no less.

commentaries.gist: Contrasts the dove, a mere bird that offered its flesh to its mate's captor, with Rama, dharma in bodily form; also recalls a monkey who rescued a hunter, reminding Sugriva of his own lineage's dharma.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rāma Varmā's Tilaka
commentaries.gist: Because a bird's conduct alone lacks scriptural force, Rama goes on to cite the authoritative verses of the sage Kandu.
Vibhishana cannot harm Rama at all; Rama, able to slay all fiends by a wish, invokes the dove as the traditional example.
Rama's speech to Sugriva on sheltering refugees, leading to Kandu's verses (chapter read for context).

practical_reading: Hospitality and protection toward someone in need should not depend on whether they have been on the 'other side'.
misreadings: As our note says: it describes the protector's duty, not a duty on the injured to host those who hurt them.
Not an endorsement of self-sacrifice to abusers.
cautions: The story involves a hunter who caught the dove's mate and the dove offering its own flesh; may be disturbing for some readers.
Do not use for readers recovering from betrayal or abuse.
speaks_to: questions of welcoming refugees, migrants or outsiders
someone deciding whether to help a former rival who is now in need
not_for: a survivor of abuse or betrayal (it can sound like 'host the one who hurt you')
research_note: The dove story itself is not told here in detail; it is told at length in the Mahabharata (Shanti Parva). We did not verify that here.

verified_ref: Valmiki Ramayana 6.18.28 (Southern Recension, itihasa.io); Baroda critical edition 6.12.15. Our id 6.18.26 is two off (itihasa 6.18.26 is Rama's introduction: 'hear the verses sung of old by the sage Kandu, son of Kanva').
attribution_note: Rama quoting the sage Kandu, to Sugriva; correct.
translation_note: Accurate. 'Kṛtātmanā' = by one of disciplined, steady mind. Note 'pareṣāṃ śaraṇaṃ gataḥ' = come for refuge from others (fleeing others), as itihasa renders it.
context: Part of Rama's argument for accepting Vibhishana. After the dove example, he quotes the sage Kandu: one must not kill an enemy who comes begging for refuge with joined palms; and here, whether he comes in distress or in pride, an enemy who seeks refuge must be protected even at the cost of one's life. Kandu adds that failing to do so from fear, delusion or desire is a sin the world condemns, and the refugee who dies unprotected takes away the protector's merit.

key_terms.sense: one who has come for refuge
even giving up one's own life

core_teaching: The duty to protect anyone who seeks refuge does not depend on their attitude or past: even a proud former enemy must be shielded, even at great personal cost.

commentaries.gist: The previous verse forbids killing a supplicant foe so as to avoid cruelty; this verse goes further and commands defending him even with one's life; failing through fear, distraction or greed is a sin all condemn.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rāma Varmā's Tilaka
commentaries.gist: Reads 'distressed or proud' as making the supplicant's merits or faults irrelevant; a disciplined person must protect him or incur sin and public blame.
Kandu's verses enjoin giving up one's transient life to save any supplicant.
Has Rama introduce the sacred verses of Kandu, son of Kanva, and conclude that refusing shelter to those who ask is a grave wrong.

practical_reading: Protection of the vulnerable should not be conditional on whether we like them or whether they come humbly.
misreadings: Not a duty imposed on the weak or wounded toward those who harmed them; it is addressed to one who has power to protect.
Not a literal call to die for anyone who asks.
cautions: 'Even at the cost of his own life' can be heavy for a reader already self-sacrificing or in a caregiving crisis.
speaks_to: those in positions of power or care (leaders, teachers, guardians)
debates about refugees and asylum
someone asked for help by a person they dislike
not_for: exhausted caregivers or people in abusive situations who may hear 'sacrifice yourself'

verified_ref: Valmiki Ramayana 6.18.33 (Southern Recension, itihasa.io); Baroda critical edition 6.12.20. Our id 6.18.31 is WRONG: this famous 'sakṛd eva prapannāya' verse is conventionally cited as Yuddha Kanda 18.33, and itihasa also numbers it 6.18.33. Itihasa 6.18.31 is the preceding verse on the great fault of not protecting those who surrender.
attribution_note: Rama to Sugriva (and the council), correct.
translation_note: Accurate. 'Sakṛd eva' = even once; 'tavāsmi' = I am yours; 'abhayaṃ sarvabhūtebhyaḥ dadāmi' = I give freedom from fear of all beings; 'etad vrataṃ mama' = this is my vow.
context: Having cited the dove and the sage Kandu, Rama concludes with his own vow: to anyone who comes to him even once and asks for protection saying 'I am yours', he grants safety from all beings. He orders Sugriva to bring the newcomer, 'whether he is Vibhishana or Ravana himself'. Vibhishana is brought, falls at Rama's feet, and is accepted.

key_terms.sense: to one who takes refuge even once

core_teaching: Rama's vow: a single sincere act of surrender, 'I am yours', is enough for him to grant complete protection. The Śrīvaiṣṇava tradition treats it as the Lord's promise of refuge (śaraṇāgati).

commentaries.gist: Rama crowns scripture, Kandu's tradition and the dove's example with his own vow: a single surrender wins fearlessness, even for Ravana in disguise.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rāma Varmā's Tilaka
commentaries.gist: The present tense 'I give' marks Rama's eternal, natural dharma; he distinguishes release from fear of rebirth for one who knows, and safety from all beings for one who says 'I am your servant'.
'This is my vow' proclaims an unconditioned resolve; Rama commands Sugriva to bring the supplicant even if it were Ravana.
Has Rama swear that any being who seeks refuge with him saying 'I am thine' is assured of his protection, whether it be Vibhishana or Ravana himself.

practical_reading: For devotees, a promise that one honest turning toward the divine is enough; in human terms, a model of offering unconditional safety to those who ask for help.
misreadings: Not a magic formula that removes all consequences; Vibhishana still serves and fights.
Not a demand on victims to protect their aggressors.
cautions: Highly devotional; secular readers may prefer the human 'protect those who ask' reading.
speaks_to: someone who feels unworthy of help or grace
a seeker beginning a spiritual practice
people afraid to ask for help
not_for: a reader who rejects devotional framing
research_note: Fix the id/ref to 6.18.33.

verified_ref: Valmiki Ramayana 6.19.6cd-7ab (Southern Recension, itihasa.io); the 'consoling him with words and drinking him in with his eyes' line (6.19.7) is a southern addition not in the Baroda critical edition. Our id 6.19.4 is two to three off.
translation_note: Accurate. Govindarāja reads 'drinking him in with his eyes' as gazing with the greatest affection.
context: Granted refuge, Vibhishana comes down from the sky with his four companions, falls at Rama's feet and says Lanka, friends and wealth are left behind and his kingdom, life and happiness now rest in Rama. Hearing this, Rama comforts him and looks at him as if drinking him in, then asks him to describe the rakshasas' strengths and weaknesses. Vibhishana tells him about Ravana, Kumbhakarna, Prahasta and Indrajit.

key_terms.sense: as if drinking him in with his eyes

core_teaching: Rama receives the one who has surrendered not coolly but with comfort and visible delight.

commentaries.gist: Rama comforts Vibhishana, apologising for the delay caused by the council's debate, and gazes on him with the utmost affection.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rāma Varmā's Tilaka
commentaries.gist: Since service in battle will come later, Rama first invites service by speech, asking for intelligence.
Notes that 6.19.6b and 7 form a single sentence.
Has Rama speak in soothing tones while seeming to consume him with his gaze.

practical_reading: When someone arrives in need, welcome them warmly and attentively before asking anything of them.
cautions: Southern-only half-verse; CE readers will not find it.
speaks_to: someone afraid of how they will be received after leaving a group, job or family
newcomers, converts, people starting over
not_for: a reader wanting an action step

verified_ref: Valmiki Ramayana 6.21.20cd-22 (Southern Recension, itihasa.io); Baroda critical edition 6.14.10-12. Our id 6.21.11 does not match; the passage spans parts of three verses (lines 'na darśayati sāmnā me...' and 'samudraṃ śoṣayiṣyāmi...' are southern additions).
translation_note: Accurate. Our Sanskrit continues with 'I will dry up the ocean; let the monkeys cross on foot', which our translation omits; worth including, since it shows the threat's purpose (a way across), not punishment for its own sake.
context: Rama has lain on kusha grass by the shore for three nights, asking the Ocean for a passage, and the Ocean has not appeared. Angered, he tells Lakshmana that his forbearance is being taken for weakness, damns patience toward such a one, calls for his bow and threatens to dry up the sea. He then shoots, the sea churns, Lakshmana tries to restrain him, and the Ocean appears, offers Nala's bridge, and Rama redirects the arrow at its request.

key_terms.sense: shame on forbearance toward such a one

core_teaching: Forbearance is a virtue, but when it is mistaken for weakness by one who will not respond to gentleness, firm action becomes appropriate.

commentaries.gist: Explains why an Ikshvaku prince sets aside patience: forbearance has its proper season and application; he also notes Rama calls for bow and arrows in stages, giving the Ocean time to relent.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Tilaka, Śiromaṇi and Bhūṣaṇa (on 6.21.19-24)
commentaries.gist: All three gloss the threatened destruction of sea-creatures and the Ocean being forced to overflow the bounds it normally keeps.
Has Rama say forbearance and gentle speech are seen as weakness by those who lack them, call for his bow, and Lakshmana try to restrain him.

practical_reading: Patience and gentleness come first, but they are not unlimited; if they are exploited, firm and clear action is legitimate, used to open the way rather than to punish.
misreadings: Not a licence for anger whenever one feels slighted; as our note says, it must be read with the three days of patient asking before and the restraint after.
Not an endorsement of destroying what stands in one's way; Rama redirects the arrow when the Ocean yields.
cautions: Contains images of killing sea-creatures; keep to the core line.
Readers who are themselves volatile may take it as permission for rage.
speaks_to: someone whose kindness keeps being exploited (at work, by a landlord, by a manipulative person)
people-pleasers learning to set firm boundaries
not_for: someone already prone to explosive anger
as a stand-alone verse without the context of prior patience

verified_ref: Valmiki Ramayana 6.34.11 (Southern Recension, itihasa.io); Baroda critical edition 6.25.11. Reference correct.
translation_note: Accurate. 'Kathā tasya' = any talk of his (Ravana's); 'niścitam' = whatever is decided; 'varo me syād anugrahaḥ' = it would be the best favour to me. Our 'line' ('not knowing is the hardest part') is an interpretive add-on but fits the preceding verses on her fear and unrest.
context: Ravana has tried to break Sita with a conjured head of Rama. Sarama, a kind rakshasi, has comforted her, explained the illusion and offered to help. Sita says Ravana bewilders her with sorcery, has her threatened and abused, and even in the grove she has no peace for fear of him. So she asks Sarama to find out whatever is being said or decided and tell her. Sarama wipes her tears and goes to learn Ravana's intentions.

key_terms.sense: that would be the greatest kindness to me

core_teaching: In fear and uncertainty, Sita asks a friend not for rescue but for the truth about what is being decided; honest information is itself a kindness.

commentaries.gist: Sita asks Sarama to report any discussion or final decision about her release or continued captivity; gentle-spoken Sarama strokes her tear-wet face and wipes away her tears.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Govindarāja, Rāma Varmā and Śivasahāya (on 6.34.9-10)
commentaries.gist: Distinguish two kinds of torment she suffers: menacing gestures (tarjana) and verbal threats (bhartsana); even in the 'sorrowless' grove she has no peace.
Has Sita ask Sarama to tell her exactly what Ravana has resolved to do.

practical_reading: When someone is anxious about decisions being made about them (a diagnosis, a court case, a job), clear, honest information is often the greatest help a friend can give.
misreadings: Not a request to spy for malice; it is a captive's plea for clarity about her own fate.
cautions: Context includes psychological abuse (threats, a fake severed head); keep context light.
speaks_to: someone waiting on decisions they cannot control (medical, legal, immigration, layoffs)
a friend wondering how to help someone anxious
not_for: someone who has said they do not want to know details yet
research_note: The itihasa synthesis for 6.34.11-12 lists no commentator tags; treat as general synthesis.

verified_ref: Valmiki Ramayana 6.59.143 (Southern Recension, itihasa.io). Not in the Baroda critical edition (a southern addition; the CE has the surrounding verses at 6.47.132-133). Our id 6.59.131 is twelve off.
translation_note: Accurate. Govindarāja reads 'gacchānujānāmi' ('go, I give you leave') at the start. The verse before (6.59.142, in the CE) gives Rama's reason: Ravana has done a great and terrible deed and struck down Rama's chief warriors, so Rama will not kill him while exhausted.
context: In their first direct battle, Ravana has struck down Lakshmana and many monkey heroes. Hanuman's blow stuns Ravana; Rama then shatters his chariot, bow and crown. Seeing him helpless and spent, Rama refuses to kill an exhausted enemy and tells him to go back to Lanka, catch his breath, and return armed to see Rama's strength. Ravana returns to Lanka humiliated, his pride broken, and wakes Kumbhakarna.

key_terms.sense: recover your breath, then come out

core_teaching: Rama will not strike an exhausted, disarmed enemy: a code of fair fighting and magnanimity in strength, combined with a clear warning.

commentaries.gist: Rama explicitly gives Ravana leave to go under his eyes, and mocks him as 'king of night-prowlers', a deceitful fighter; he spares him to avoid the reproach of killing a battle-weary foe.
Rama bids him rest in Lanka and come back with chariot and bow to witness his might.
Seeing Ravana with no other refuge, compassionate Rama only cuts off his crown, breaking his pride and leaving him like a fangless serpent.
Has Rama tell the weary Ravana he will not deliver him to death, grant him a reprieve to return to Lanka, and invite him back to test his prowess.

practical_reading: Strength is shown in restraint: do not press an advantage against someone who is spent; give them room to recover, even in a contest.
misreadings: As our note says, it is a warrior's fairness and a warning, not gentle advice to rest.
Not forgiveness or reconciliation; the war continues.
cautions: Our 'line' ('Go and rest. I know you're exhausted. Come back when you're ready.') reads like self-care advice; that drifts from the verse, which is said to an enemy with a challenge attached.
speaks_to: someone in a position of advantage over a rival or opponent
competitors, litigants, managers in conflict
sport and fair play
not_for: someone exhausted who wants permission to rest (the verse is spoken to an enemy, with a threat)
research_note: Southern-only verse; if the app cites CE numbering, it does not exist there.

verified_ref: Valmiki Ramayana 6.63.4 (Southern Recension, itihasa.io); Baroda critical edition 6.51.4. Reference correct.
translation_note: Accurate. 'Anubandhaḥ' = consequence, what follows from an act; 'vīryadarpeṇa' = through pride in one's own strength.
context: With the war going badly, Ravana has had his giant brother Kumbhakarna woken from months-long sleep and laments his losses. Kumbhakarna laughs: this is the disaster the council foresaw when Ravana ignored his well-wishers (meaning Vibhishana). The fruit of the sinful deed has come quickly. Here he says the act was never thought through at the outset; out of pride in strength alone its consequences were never weighed. He goes on to lecture on right order in policy, then, loyal, agrees to fight.
core_teaching: Ravana's disaster came from acting on pride in his strength without weighing the consequences beforehand.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of the three commentators (on 6.63.2-4)
commentaries.gist: All identify the 'earlier counsel' with the council where Vibhishana spoke, read 'ignoring well-wishers' as disregarding them; Tilaka and Bhūṣaṇa cite a dictionary sense of 'anubandha' as the arising of harm, i.e. Ravana never weighed what abducting Sita would bring.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Tilaka and Bhūṣaṇa
commentaries.gist: Cite the maxim that extreme merit or sin bears fruit in this very life, explaining how swiftly Ravana's wrong has caught up with him.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rāma Varmā's Tilaka (on 6.63.1)
commentaries.gist: Kumbhakarna laughs because Ravana is reaping the fruit of rejecting Vibhishana's advice.
Has Kumbhakarna say Ravana did not reflect at first on what might happen and, proud of his strength, overlooked the consequences.

practical_reading: Before a big decision, especially one driven by confidence or pride, sit down and trace where it leads.
misreadings: Not 'I told you so' for its own sake; Kumbhakarna still fights for his brother.
cautions: Speaker is a rakshasa criticising a brother; for a reader blaming themselves for a past decision, it may sting.
speaks_to: leaders and founders reviewing a failed decision
someone tempted by an impulsive, prideful move
not_for: someone already full of regret about a past choice (can deepen self-blame)

verified_ref: Valmiki Ramayana 6.63.5 (Southern Recension, itihasa.io); Baroda critical edition 6.51.5. Reference correct.
translation_note: Accurate. 'Aiśvaryam āsthitaḥ' = relying on his power/position; 'nayānayau' = good policy and bad.
context: Continuing his rebuke after being woken, Kumbhakarna says a ruler who, relying on his power, does later what should come first and first what should come later, cannot tell good policy from bad. He adds that acts done out of place and time are spoiled like offerings poured into unconsecrated fires, and describes the right way: deliberate with ministers first. Then he agrees to fight for his brother.
