key_terms.sense: what should come first / what should come after

core_teaching: Order matters: deliberation should precede action. A leader who acts first and consults afterward has lost the ability to judge.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rāma Varmā's Tilaka and Govindarāja's Bhūṣaṇa
commentaries.gist: Deliberation and consultation are the 'prior' duty and action the 'later'; inverting them ruins statecraft like oblations poured into unconsecrated fires.
Reads the simile as offerings poured into very unworthy recipients.
Has Kumbhakarna say one who, trusting his own power, leaves until last what should be first, or does first what should follow, cannot tell wise from foolish.

practical_reading: Consult and plan before acting, not after; when a decision has gone wrong, check whether the steps were taken in the wrong order.
misreadings: Not a rule against ever acting quickly; it targets acting on power without prior deliberation.
speaks_to: managers, founders, parents making big decisions
someone about to act before consulting the people affected
not_for: a reader needing comfort rather than critique
research_note: Our note says 'counsel should have come before the abduction, not after'; this matches the commentators' reading.

verified_ref: Valmiki Ramayana 6.65.4 (Southern Recension, itihasa.io); Baroda critical edition 6.53.4. Reference correct.
attribution_note: Kumbhakarna, addressing Ravana after rebuking Mahodara; correct.
translation_note: Accurate on the Tilaka/Śiromaṇi reading. Govindarāja reads it differently: a hero neither tolerates an insult from others nor esteems himself boastfully. Our rendering follows the majority.
context: Mahodara, a courtier, has argued against Kumbhakarna fighting alone and proposed a scheme instead. Kumbhakarna rebukes him and tells Ravana he will rid him of his fear by killing Rama today: heroes don't thunder in vain like rainless clouds; they don't praise themselves but do hard deeds without display. He adds that Mahodara's counsel would please only timid, foolish kings who think themselves wise, then goes to battle, where he dies.

key_terms.sense: they cannot bear, will not tolerate
to praise themselves with their own mouths

core_teaching: Real courage shows itself in hard deeds, not in boasting.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rāma Varmā's Tilaka and Śivasahāya's Śiromaṇi
commentaries.gist: Valiant men cannot bear to praise themselves with their own tongues; they achieve hard feats without displaying their ability in words.
Reads the verbs as collective singulars: a hero neither tolerates insult from others nor esteems himself highly.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of the three commentators (on 6.65.3)
commentaries.gist: Contrast empty boasting with action, using the image of rainless autumn clouds that rumble but do not wet the earth.
Has Kumbhakarna say heroes do not thunder in vain like rainless clouds, need not boast, and achieve the hardest feats without bluster.

practical_reading: Let your work speak; when tempted to announce or overclaim, do the hard thing quietly instead.
misreadings: Not an endorsement of Kumbhakarna's cause; he fights for Ravana's unjust war.
Not a rule against ever acknowledging one's achievements.
cautions: Speaker dies soon after in an unjust war; the maxim is sound, the context ironic.
speaks_to: people tempted to self-promote or over-promise
teams with a culture of talk over delivery
someone quietly doing hard work unnoticed
not_for: someone with low self-worth who needs to learn to name their strengths
research_note: Our listener field says 'Mahodara and Ravana'; the verse is addressed to Ravana right after rebuking Mahodara, so this is fair.

verified_ref: Valmiki Ramayana 6.102.22cd-23ab (Southern Recension, itihasa.io; sarga 102 in this numbering). Not in the Baroda critical edition (this lament, 6.102.19-24, is a southern addition). Our id 6.101.18 reflects the shorter Yuddha numbering (which runs about one sarga behind here).
attribution_note: Rama to the fallen Lakshmana, correct.
translation_note: Accurate. 'Pramattasya' here is better 'distraught, beside myself' than 'careless'; Śiromaṇi reads Rama as recalling that Lakshmana alone consoled him in every sorrow.
context: Ravana's spear has struck down Lakshmana. Rama, distraught, says victory means nothing without his brother, wonders what wrong he did to deserve this, and begs Lakshmana to rise and look at him: in the mountains and forests, whenever Rama was grief-stricken and despairing, Lakshmana was the one who consoled him. The physician Sushena then assures Rama that Lakshmana is still alive and sends Hanuman for the healing herbs; Lakshmana recovers.

key_terms.sense: the one who consoled, gave me breath again

core_teaching: In his own grief Rama recognises who had carried him through his darkest times: his brother, his consoler.

commentaries.gist: The first 'look' means 'wake up', the second 'look at me'; Rama recalls that throughout their forest wanderings Lakshmana alone consoled him in every sorrow.
Explains how the sinless Rama can ask what wrong he did in another birth: he takes it to mean, what wrong did I ever do this rakshasa that he struck down my brother?
Sushena steps forward to steady the grief-stricken Rama and urges him to set aside despondency.
Has Rama say wives and friends may be found anywhere, but nowhere so dear a brother; Sushena then comforts him.

practical_reading: Name and thank the people who held you up in your low moments, before a crisis forces you to.
misreadings: Not proof that Lakshmana died; he recovers in the same sarga.
cautions: A lament over a seemingly dead brother; for someone grieving a sibling it can be powerful but raw.
Our 'line' ('you were the one who lifted me up') is fine; the verse's speaker is in acute grief, not reflective gratitude.
speaks_to: gratitude to a sibling, friend or partner who stood by you
fear of losing someone who has always supported you
caregivers' and patients' families
not_for: someone whose sibling has just died (the story's recovery may feel cruel by contrast)
research_note: Southern-only passage; our 6.101 sarga number is the shorter-numbering edition's, itihasa has 6.102.

verified_ref: Valmiki Ramayana 6.112.17 (Southern Recension, itihasa.io). Not in the Baroda critical edition (6.112.14-19 are southern additions). Our id 6.109.15 follows a shorter numbering three sargas behind itihasa here.
attribution_note: Rama to the grieving Vibhishana, correct.
translation_note: Accurate. Our 'line' ('Sometimes you win, and sometimes you fall') generalises from battle to life, which is how teachers use it; the verse itself is about warriors in war.
context: Ravana is dead. Vibhishana weeps over his brother. Rama consoles him: Ravana did not fall feebly but undaunted, and warriors true to their code who die in battle are not to be mourned; no one has ever had only victory in war, since a hero either kills or is killed. This is the settled path of warriors, so Vibhishana should set aside his fever of grief and think of what must be done next (the funeral rites).

key_terms.sense: has ever existed at any time

key_terms.term: parair vā hanyate ... parān vā hanti
key_terms.sense: either he is struck by others or he strikes them

core_teaching: In battle no one wins always; a warrior either falls or fells others, so a fighter's death in war is part of the path he chose, not a disgrace.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Śivasahāya's Śiromaṇi and Govindarāja's Bhūṣaṇa
commentaries.gist: Even defeat in combat is no cause for sorrow, because unbroken one-sided victory has never existed: a hero either slays his enemies or is slain.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rāma Varmā's Tilaka and Śiromaṇi (on 6.112.18)
commentaries.gist: Rama invokes the teaching of Manu and the ancients that death in battle is the warrior's honoured path, so a warrior killed in combat is not to be mourned.
Has Rama tell Vibhishana that no one is always victorious in war; sometimes the brave fall, sometimes the foe.

practical_reading: Loss is part of any real contest; one defeat does not undo a life of effort, and no one wins every time.
misreadings: Not 'don't grieve'; Rama acknowledges the dead man's courage before guiding Vibhishana to the rites.
Not a glorification of war.
cautions: Said over a dead body to a grieving brother, as part of an argument that warriors are 'not to be mourned'. On a grief plan this would land badly; it fits better in a plan on failure and resilience.
Southern-only verse.
speaks_to: someone after a defeat (a lost election, case, match, deal)
athletes, litigants, entrepreneurs
not_for: someone grieving a death, especially a violent one
families of soldiers killed in action, unless they invite this framing

verified_ref: Valmiki Ramayana 6.112.25 (Southern Recension, itihasa.io). Not in the Baroda critical edition (6.112.20-25 are southern additions, per itihasa.io's concordance). Our id 6.109.23 follows a shorter numbering three sargas behind itihasa here.
translation_note: Accurate. 'Nirvṛttaṃ naḥ prayojanam' = our purpose is done; 'mamāpy eṣa yathā tava' = he is mine just as he is yours.
context: After Rama's words of consolation, Vibhishana hesitates over Ravana's rites; in the Southern text he then recalls Ravana's generosity, Vedic fires, austerities and learning and asks, by Rama's grace, to perform his funeral. Moved, Rama gives the famous answer: enmity ends with death, our purpose is achieved, let his rites be done; he is now as much mine as yours. Ravana is cremated with royal honours and Mandodari and the queens lament.

key_terms.sense: he is mine as he is yours

core_teaching: Once the wrong has been stopped, enmity should end with death; the fallen enemy is owed honour and proper rites.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Govindarāja's Bhūṣaṇa and Rāma Varmā's Tilaka
commentaries.gist: Rama forestalls Vibhishana's hesitation: enmity ends at death, since Ravana can do no more harm and Rama's vow is fulfilled; so the rites must proceed, and in death Ravana is as dear to Rama as to Vibhishana.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of the three commentators (on 6.112.24)
commentaries.gist: Because all Ravana's sons had died, Vibhishana is chief mourner; Rama, moved by his plea, magnanimously orders the funeral rites.
Has Rama say death has ended their enmity, Ravana is as dear to him as to Vibhishana, and the obsequies should be performed.

practical_reading: Let quarrels end with death: honour the dead, even those you opposed, and help the living mourn them.
misreadings: As our note says: the enmity ends after the wrong has been stopped, not before; it is not a demand to forgive an ongoing abuser.
Not a demand that survivors feel warmly toward someone who harmed them.
cautions: For a reader grieving someone who hurt them, 'he is mine as much as yours' may be healing or may feel like pressure; offer gently.
Not in the critical edition, despite being widely quoted.
speaks_to: someone attending the funeral of an estranged parent or relative
families divided by old quarrels at a death
people unsure whether they may mourn someone who wronged them
not_for: someone whose abuser is still alive and active
research_note: Widely quoted maxim, but itihasa.io marks it as southern-only (not in the Baroda CE). Worth noting if the app ever cites CE numbering.

verified_ref: Valmiki Ramayana 6.114.15cd-16ab (Southern Recension, itihasa.io); Baroda critical edition 6.99.9. Our id 6.111.11 follows a shorter numbering three sargas behind itihasa here.
attribution_note: Mandodari to the dead Ravana, correct.
translation_note: Accurate. 'Indriyāṇi purā jitvā' refers, per Tilaka and Śiromaṇi, to Ravana's ancient austerities to win Brahma's boons; 'smaradbhir iva tad vairam' = as if remembering that old enmity.
context: Over Ravana's body, his chief queen Mandodari laments. She has just declared that Rama was Vishnu in human form who slew Ravana for the world's good. Here she names the deeper cause: long ago Ravana conquered his senses (through austerities) and so conquered the three worlds; now those same senses, as if avenging that old defeat, have conquered him. She goes on to recall the signs she saw (Khara's death, Hanuman's entry into Lanka) and her own unheeded pleas to make peace with Rama.
core_teaching: Ravana's power came from early self-mastery; his fall came when he let his senses rule him again. Self-control won is not self-control kept.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rāma Varmā's Tilaka and Śivasahāya's Śiromaṇi
commentaries.gist: In his ancient penances to please Brahma, Ravana forcibly subdued his senses and so won the three worlds; now those senses, as if bearing a grudge, drove him to illicit passion and defeated him.
Mandodari recalls the signs of Rama's divinity she saw, and that she did urge peace by returning Sita, which Ravana spurned.
Has Mandodari say that having once subdued his senses he conquered the three worlds, and afterwards his senses conquered him in turn.

practical_reading: Discipline that built success can erode quietly; the habits we once mastered can master us if we stop watching them.
misreadings: Not a claim that desire itself is evil; the point is losing mastery.
Not Mandodari gloating; it is a widow's grief-stricken insight.
cautions: Spoken by a widow over her husband's corpse; for a reader recently widowed, the setting may be painful.
Relates Ravana's fall to his desire for another man's wife; keep framing general.
speaks_to: someone who once had strong discipline and has slipped (addiction, habits, ethics)
high achievers at risk of complacency
not_for: someone in early recovery who could hear it as fatalistic
recent widows or widowers

verified_ref: Valmiki Ramayana 6.116.44-46 (three verses; Southern Recension, itihasa.io); Baroda critical edition 6.101.35-37. Our id 6.113.29 follows a shorter numbering three sargas behind itihasa here, and covers three verses.
attribution_note: Sita to Hanuman, correct. The first verse is a saying she quotes (a bear's verse sung near a tiger).
translation_note: Accurate in substance. In verse 44, 'na paraḥ pāpam ādatte pareṣāṃ pāpakarmaṇām' is read by the commentators as 'a noble person does not retaliate for (take on) the sins of wrongdoers'; 'samaya' = the moral pledge or standard. 'Na kaścin nāparādhyati' = there is no one who does not err (Tilaka and Śiromaṇi: everyone errs somehow). Our 'line' ('No one is without fault') is good.
context: After Ravana's death, Hanuman brings Sita news of victory and offers to kill the rakshasis who tormented her for months. Sita refuses: they acted on Ravana's orders and no longer threaten her, and she accepts what happened as her lot. She quotes an old saying sung by a bear who, though betrayed by a hunter he had sheltered, refused to give him up to a tiger: the noble do not return evil for evil. Hanuman praises her as Rama's worthy wife and takes her message to Rama.

key_terms.sense: the noble do not repay wrong with wrong
the good are adorned by their conduct
there is no one who never errs

core_teaching: Sita, now free and able to punish, chooses compassion: the noble keep their own standard of conduct and do not answer cruelty with cruelty, since everyone errs.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of the three commentators (on 6.116.43-44)
commentaries.gist: All recount the parable behind the saying: a hunter chased by a tiger was sheltered by a bear in a tree, tried to push the sleeping bear down at the tiger's urging, yet the bear still refused to hand him over.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rāma Varmā's Tilaka and Śivasahāya's Śiromaṇi
commentaries.gist: Resolve the double negative as 'every person errs in some way', grounding compassion in shared fallibility.
Says this sarga reveals Sita's supreme compassion, her patience with offenders, and her role as mediator; links 'worthy of Rama' to Rama's own vow of refuge.
Has Sita say the women acted under orders, cite the ancient saying that a superior being does not render evil for evil, and ask who is without fault.

practical_reading: When you finally have power over those who hurt you, choose not to become like them; protect yourself, but do not seek revenge.
misreadings: Not a demand that victims stay near or reconcile with those who harmed them; Sita is now safe and her tormentors powerless.
Not saying the guards' cruelty was acceptable.
Sita's 'it was my lot / fate' framing (6.116.41) should not be used to tell a victim their suffering was deserved.
cautions: Context is months of threats and abuse; for a survivor of abuse, present it as freedom from revenge, never as an obligation to forgive or excuse.
Three verses under one id.
speaks_to: someone tempted to retaliate now that they have the upper hand
a person ready to let go of revenge after a hurt
managers dealing with those who wronged them under orders
not_for: someone currently being harmed
a recent survivor of abuse who is not ready to think about compassion for the abuser

verified_ref: Valmiki Ramayana 6.119.10 (Southern Recension, itihasa.io); Baroda critical edition 6.104.10. Our id 6.116.10 follows a shorter numbering three sargas behind itihasa here.
translation_note: Accurate. 'Saha saṃvṛddhabhāvena' = through love that grew together (Tilaka: mutual love since youth); 'hatā tenāsmi śāśvatam' = by that I am destroyed forever. 'Mānada' (giver of honour) is a pointed vocative in context.
context: After the victory Rama, before the assembled army, tells Sita he fought to clear his family's name, not for her, and that he cannot take her back after she lived in another man's house. Shocked, Sita answers: why speak to me like a common man to a common woman? Her heart was always his; what Ravana did to her body was against her will. If after their love grown together and their long life together he still does not know her, she is lost forever. She asks why he did not reject her when Hanuman came, which would have spared everyone a war, then asks Lakshmana for a pyre and enters the fire; Agni returns her unharmed.

key_terms.sense: by love that grew up together

core_teaching: Sita protests with dignity that a long shared life should have taught Rama who she is; being unknown by the one closest to you is a permanent wound.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rāma Varmā's Tilaka
commentaries.gist: Reads 'saha saṃvṛddhabhāva' as mutual love grown since youth; on the preceding verse, has Sita say her heart was always Rama's, and her limbs were not hers to command.
Sita objects to being judged by the conduct of other women when her own nature has already been tested; she had no will over a body seized by another.
Sita asks why Rama did not tell her through Hanuman that he would not take her back; she would have ended her life then and spared the war.
Has Sita ask why he speaks to her as a common man to an ordinary woman, insist her heart stayed faithful, and lament that he has cast aside her love.

practical_reading: Gives words to the pain of being misjudged by someone who should know you best, and models answering with dignity rather than collapse.
misreadings: As our note says: use her protest; do not present the fire ordeal as a model.
Not evidence that a partner's suspicion is justified.
cautions: Context is a public accusation of sexual impurity against a survivor of abduction, followed by self-immolation; handle with great care.
The following verses mention her wish to have ended her life; avoid quoting them.
May trigger readers who have experienced victim-blaming, sexual violence or a partner's distrust.
speaks_to: someone misjudged or disbelieved by a spouse, parent or close friend
survivors who were not believed
the grief of feeling unknown in a long relationship
not_for: someone being urged to 'prove' their loyalty to a controlling partner
as an ideal of wifely endurance

verified_ref: Valmiki Ramayana 6.124.18-19 (two verses; Southern Recension, itihasa.io); Baroda critical edition 6.109.17-18. Our id 6.121.16 follows a shorter numbering three sargas behind itihasa here.
translation_note: Accurate. The double negative 'na khalv etan na kuryām' = it is surely not that I would not do as you ask. Śiromaṇi and Bhūṣaṇa read verses 18-20 as one sentence, so Rama also longs to see Kausalya, Sumitra, Kaikeyi, Guha and the people.
context: After the victory Vibhishana, now king of Lanka, begs Rama to stay, bathe, be adorned and accept his hospitality, offering the Pushpaka chariot for an easy return. Before both armies Rama says he is already honoured by Vibhishana's counsel and friendship; it is not that he refuses, but his heart hurries to see Bharata, who came to Chitrakuta to bring him back and whose bowed plea he did not grant, and his mothers and people. He asks Vibhishana's leave and not to be hurt. Vibhishana summons the Pushpaka.

key_terms.sense: it is not that I would refuse
of him who begged with bowed head
whose words I did not carry out

core_teaching: Rama gently declines honours because his heart is set on reuniting with the brother whose plea he once had to refuse; love and an old debt of feeling outweigh celebration.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Śiromaṇi and Govindarāja's Bhūṣaṇa
commentaries.gist: Link verse 18 with 19-20 as one sentence: Rama assures Vibhishana he would never slight his request, yet his mind runs ahead to Bharata and his mothers.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rāma Varmā's Tilaka and Śiromaṇi
commentaries.gist: Explain why Rama cannot delay even briefly for the banquet: Bharata travelled to Chitrakuta and begged with bowed head, and Rama refused him.
Rama counts the gift of the Pushpaka as the highest hospitality already received, and asks Vibhishana not to feel hurt or angry.
Has Rama say he cannot accept because his heart urges him to see Bharata, who came to Chitrakuta and whose appeal he did not heed.

practical_reading: It is fine to decline a kind invitation gracefully when the heart is called home; say thank you, explain, and go to the people who are waiting for you.
misreadings: Not ingratitude toward Vibhishana; Rama honours him publicly first.
cautions: Two verses merged.
speaks_to: someone torn between an honour or opportunity and returning to family
homesick migrants, students, soldiers
reconciliation with a sibling after a hard parting
not_for: someone who has no home or family to return to (may sting)

verified_ref: Valmiki Ramayana 6.128.17 (Southern Recension, itihasa.io); Baroda critical edition 6.113.16. Our id 6.125.12 follows a shorter numbering three sargas behind itihasa here.
translation_note: Accurate on the face-value reading. 'Saṃgatyā' = through long association (with power). Govindarāja reads it very differently (see commentaries). Our 'line' ('I won't fight family for it') goes beyond the verse but fits Tilaka/Śiromaṇi's gloss that Rama would go and live elsewhere.
context: Approaching Ayodhya on the Pushpaka, Rama stops at Bharadvaja's hermitage and sends Hanuman ahead, in human form, to tell Guha and Bharata of his return and to watch Bharata's face, eyes and words closely: an ancestral kingdom rich in everything might sway anyone's mind. If Bharata now wants the kingdom for himself, let him rule it all. Hanuman finds Bharata at Nandigrama, thin, in bark clothes, ruling in the name of Rama's sandals, and overjoyed at the news.

key_terms.sense: inner signs, demeanour (from the previous verse)

core_teaching: Rama will not contest the throne with his brother: if Bharata has come to want it, he may keep it. He checks the facts first rather than assuming.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rāma Varmā's Tilaka and Śivasahāya's Śiromaṇi
commentaries.gist: Take the verse at face value: even a good mind can be swayed by long familiarity with power or by Kaikeyi's company; if so, Rama will gladly let Bharata rule and spend his own days elsewhere.
Rejects any suspicion of Bharata as contrary to both brothers' natures; Rama actually hopes that, in the joy of reunion, Bharata might now accept the crown as Rama had urged at Chitrakuta.
Govindarāja reads Rama's instruction as finding out whether Bharata would accept the crown or firmly refuse; all agree Hanuman should return before the party travels far.
Rama sends Hanuman to Ayodhya to learn how all fare and to give Bharata the news; Hanuman finds Bharata in ascetic dress ruling with the sandals before him.

practical_reading: Before assuming the worst about family over money or property, find out how they really feel; and be willing to let go rather than fight over inheritance.
misreadings: Not evidence that Rama distrusted Bharata; Govindarāja explicitly rejects that reading.
Not advice to give up what is rightfully yours in every situation.
cautions: Readers in real inheritance disputes may hear it as 'just give in'; offer as a value, not a rule.
speaks_to: siblings navigating inheritance, a family business, or caregiving roles
someone returning to a role another has filled in their absence
not_for: someone being exploited by a relative over property

verified_ref: Valmiki Ramayana 6.130.54cd-55 (Southern Recension, itihasa.io); Baroda critical edition 6.115.43-44. Our id 6.127.38 follows a shorter numbering three sargas behind itihasa here.
translation_note: Accurate. 'Nyāsa' = a deposit held in trust; 'niryātitam' = handed back to its owner; 'adya janma kṛtārthaṃ me' = today my birth has achieved its purpose. The next verse (kingdom increased tenfold) is not part of our text.
context: Rama arrives at Nandigrama. Bharata, who ruled for fourteen years as a hermit in Rama's name with Rama's sandals on the throne, welcomes him with the citizens and the queen mothers. He places the sandals back on Rama's feet and, with joined palms, hands back the kingdom he held in trust: today his life has meaning, seeing Rama back as king. He invites Rama to inspect the treasury, granaries and army, all increased tenfold. The monkeys and Vibhishana weep at such brotherly love.

key_terms.sense: today my life has fulfilled its purpose
and my heart's wish has come true

core_teaching: Bharata, who never claimed the throne as his, returns it intact as a trust kept faithfully; fulfilment for him is seeing Rama restored.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rāma Varmā's Tilaka and Govindarāja's Bhūṣaṇa
commentaries.gist: Gloss 'nyāsa' as a pledged deposit entrusted for safekeeping, and 'niryātita' as duly returned to its rightful owner.
Adds that the kingdom has been faithfully guarded all this time.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Tilaka and Bhūṣaṇa (on 6.130.57)
commentaries.gist: The onlookers weep for joy that such brothers exist and in sorrow at the contrast with their own families' fratricidal strife (Vali and Sugriva, Ravana and Vibhishana).
Has Bharata say he renders back the kingdom received in trust, that his life's purpose is fulfilled, and that by Rama's grace he has increased everything tenfold.

practical_reading: Hold what is entrusted to you as a trust, not a possession, and hand it back gladly, in better shape than you received it.
misreadings: Not about servility; Bharata's role is honoured as dharma at its highest.
speaks_to: caretakers of a family business, property, or role during someone's absence
stewards, trustees, interim leaders
the end of a long wait for someone's return
not_for: someone whose loved one will not return (the reunion may sting)
research_note: Our prasang says Bharata, on hearing Rama is near, quotes 'a person who stays alive will find joy, even after a hundred years'. We did not locate this in the passages read (itihasa 6.128 or Shastri 6.128); it may be in the following sarga. Unverified.

verified_ref: Valmiki Ramayana 7.40.10 (Southern Recension, itihasa.io); Baroda critical edition 7.39.11. Our id 7.40.6 is four off.
translation_note: Accurate. 'Smartavyaḥ parayā prītyā' = I should be remembered with the highest love; 'vigatajvaraḥ' = free of fever/anxiety. Our 'my only request' is a gloss; the verse just says 'and I, with Sugriva, should be remembered'.
context: After the coronation, Rama sends his allies home. He has told Sugriva to rule Kishkindha and cherish his companions, and embraced him repeatedly. Now he tells Vibhishana to rule Lanka by dharma, never let his mind turn to unrighteousness, and always remember Rama and Sugriva with love; then go, free of worry. The assembly applauds. Hanuman then asks his boon.
core_teaching: Rama's parting wish to a friend: rule rightly, and keep the bond alive in memory with love.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of the three commentators (on 7.40.9-10)
commentaries.gist: Śiromaṇi glosses wise kings as those with dharma-guided judgement; Tilaka and Govindarāja read 'dhruvam' as for a long time.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rāma Varmā's Tilaka
commentaries.gist: Finds a veiled warning in asking to be remembered with Sugriva: Vibhishana must never take on Ravana's arrogance, or Rama and Sugriva would deal with him as they did with Ravana.
Rama, having embraced Sugriva again and again, speaks affectionately to Vibhishana as he sends his allies home.

practical_reading: At partings, ask only to be remembered with love, and send friends off free of worry.
misreadings: Tilaka's 'veiled warning' reading shows the line is not only sentimental; it also reminds a new ruler of accountability.
speaks_to: farewells: friends moving away, colleagues leaving, graduations
long-distance friendships
not_for: fresh bereavement (being 'remembered' can sound like a death)

verified_ref: Valmiki Ramayana 7.40.17 (Southern Recension, itihasa.io). Not in the Baroda critical edition (7.40.16-17 are southern additions). Our id 7.40.10 is seven off.
translation_note: Accurate. 'Utkaṇṭhā' = yearning, ache of separation; 'meghalekhā' = a streak or bank of cloud; 'caryāmṛtam' = the nectar of your deeds. The previous verse says the apsarases will recite the story to him.
context: As the allies take leave, Hanuman asks a boon: may his love and devotion stay fixed on Rama, and may he live as long as Rama's story is told on earth; may celestial women recite it to him, and hearing the nectar of Rama's deeds, he will dispel his longing as the wind scatters clouds. Rama rises from the throne, embraces him and grants it, and gives him his own necklace.

key_terms.sense: as the wind scatters a line of cloud

core_teaching: For Hanuman, hearing Rama's story is how he bears separation from Rama; the story keeps the beloved present.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rāma Varmā's Tilaka
commentaries.gist: Glosses Hanuman's longing as the yearning to be with Rama.
Glosses the longing as the hard-to-bear sorrow born of parting, which the recited story will scatter like a breeze dispersing a thin cloud.
Has Hanuman ask that the Apsaras recount Rama's history to him, so the nectar of his deeds will dispel his anxieties as wind chases clouds.

practical_reading: When separated from someone or something you love, return to their story; telling and hearing it can ease the ache.
misreadings: Not an escape from life; Hanuman's listening is devotion that sustains him.
cautions: Southern-only verse.
speaks_to: missing a loved one far away
devotees who find comfort in kathā, bhajan or reading
grief that seeks comfort in memories and stories
not_for: readers who want no devotional framing
research_note: Our note calls this 'the root of katha-shravana as practice'; that is an interpretive claim we did not find in the commentary syntheses.

verified_ref: Valmiki Ramayana 7.40.19-21 (Southern Recension, itihasa.io); Baroda critical edition 7.39.18 for 19-20; 7.40.21 ('ekaikasyopakārasya...') is a southern addition. Our id 7.40.12 is seven off and covers three-plus verses. The lines in our Sanskrit 'śeṣasyehopakārāṇāṃ bhavāma ṛṇino vayam' and 'madaṅge jīrṇatāṃ yātu yat tvayopakṛtaṃ kape' are NOT in itihasa.io's text; Shastri's translation does have equivalents (remaining a debtor; the memory abiding in Rama's heart), so they belong to another southern version.
translation_note: Faithful to our Sanskrit. Note: in itihasa's reading 21cd is 'naraḥ pratyupakārāṇām āpatsv āyāti pātratām' = a person becomes fit to receive a return favour only in adversity; our 'a person needs repaying only in times of trouble' matches. 'May what you have done for me be digested within me' (jīrṇatāṃ yātu) is traditionally understood as 'may your kindnesses stay unrepaid in me', i.e. may you never be in trouble.
context: Hanuman has asked to live as long as Rama's story is told. Rama rises, embraces him and grants it: as long as the worlds last, the story will last, and with it Hanuman's fame and life. Then he says that for each of Hanuman's services he would give his life, and hopes he never has to repay, since one repays only when the benefactor is in trouble. He places his own pearl necklace on Hanuman's chest.

key_terms.sense: as long as the story circulates
for each single service I would give my life
becomes the recipient (of repayment) in times of trouble

core_teaching: Rama grants Hanuman life as long as his story lasts, and declares a debt of gratitude he hopes never to repay, because repaying would mean Hanuman had fallen into misfortune.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rāma Varmā's Tilaka and Śivasahāya's Śiromaṇi (on 7.40.21)
commentaries.gist: A person becomes eligible for a return favour only in calamity; so wishing to repay a benefactor amounts to wishing him distress, and Rama silently prays misfortune never touches Hanuman.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of the three commentators (on 7.40.19-20)
commentaries.gist: Rama ratifies the boon: as long as the worlds endure the story endures, and with it Hanuman's fame and life; Tilaka says this grants Hanuman permanence for the whole cosmic age.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of the three commentators (on 7.40.22-23)
commentaries.gist: Rama then fastens his moon-bright pearl necklace with a cat's-eye centre on Hanuman, who glows like golden Meru crowned by the moon.
Has Rama say he would give his life for every service and still remain Hanuman's debtor, that the memory will ever abide in his heart, and that one turns to those one has helped in misfortune.

practical_reading: Some kindnesses cannot be repaid; carry them as a grateful debt and wish your benefactor never to need anything from you.
misreadings: Not a refusal to repay kindness; it is a wish that the friend never be in need.
cautions: Text varies between editions; if quoting the Sanskrit, note that two lines are not in the itihasa.io southern text.
speaks_to: deep gratitude toward a mentor, parent, friend
someone who has been helped greatly and cannot repay
not_for: someone carrying unhealthy obligation or guilt toward a benefactor
research_note: Our Sanskrit combines lines from different recensions; the brief asked for checks, and this is one to fix or annotate.

verified_ref: Valmiki Ramayana 7.48.6 (Southern Recension, itihasa.io); Baroda critical edition 7.47.6. Reference correct.
translation_note: Accurate. 'Vijanīkṛtā' = made alone, cut off from people; 'duḥkhaparāyaṇā' = wholly given over to sorrow.
context: Lakshmana, in anguish, has just told Sita on the bank of the Ganga that Rama has abandoned her because of public gossip about her time in Lanka, and that he must leave her near Valmiki's hermitage. Sita, pregnant, faints, then speaks: her body seems made for sorrow; what sin did she commit? Before, she lived in the forest happily following Rama; now how can she live alone, and to whom will she tell her grief? She adds she cannot drown herself, because Rama's line would end with her child.

key_terms.sense: made solitary, cut off from everyone
to whom shall I tell it

core_teaching: Sita voices the loneliness of an innocent person cast out: the worst of the exile is having no one to share her sorrow with.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rāma Varmā's Tilaka and Govindarāja's Bhūṣaṇa (on 7.48.5-6)
commentaries.gist: Contrast this solitary banishment with the earlier forest exile, which she bore gladly as long as she followed Rama.
Reads a devotional nuance: with Rama present, even apparent suffering was joy; without him, she is alone with her grief.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Tilaka and Śiromaṇi (on 7.48.7)
commentaries.gist: She cannot answer the sages who will ask why she was cast off, because she committed no wrong to justify it.
Has Sita ask how, abandoned by all, she can live in solitude, and to whom she will confide her affliction.

practical_reading: Names the particular pain of isolation in sorrow; the first help for someone cast out is someone to listen.
misreadings: Not a sign that she deserved it; the commentators stress she committed no wrong.
cautions: The next verses mention her thought of drowning herself in the Ganga (rejected for her unborn child); do not quote them to a vulnerable reader.
Pregnancy and abandonment by a spouse; sensitive for readers facing separation, divorce or single parenthood.
speaks_to: someone newly isolated by divorce, migration, illness or family rejection
the loneliness of grief with no one to talk to
not_for: a reader in active crisis without a pointer to real support

verified_ref: Valmiki Ramayana 7.48.15cd-16ab (Southern Recension, itihasa.io); Baroda critical edition 7.47.12. Our id 7.48.14 is one to two off.
attribution_note: Sita to Lakshmana, as a message for Rama; correct.
translation_note: Accurate. 'Svaśarīram' = my own body/person; she does not grieve for her own plight so much as for the citizens' slander. The surrounding message (treat the citizens as brothers; a husband is a woman's deity, so his wish must be done even at the cost of life) frames her composure as wifely duty.
context: Composing herself, Sita gives Lakshmana a message for Rama: he knows she is pure and devoted; she has been abandoned out of his fear of ill fame, and it is her part to ward off reproach from him. He should treat the citizens as his brothers, which is his highest dharma. She does not grieve for herself as much as for the people's slander. She adds that a husband is a woman's god, kinsman and teacher, asks Lakshmana to look at her (visibly pregnant) and leave. Lakshmana bows, unable to speak.

key_terms.sense: I do not grieve for my own person

core_teaching: Sita, though wronged, speaks with composure: what grieves her most is not her own hardship but the false talk that caused it.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rāma Varmā's Tilaka
commentaries.gist: Reads the message as turning to statecraft: Rama should treat citizens like brothers, and act so as to remain free of public reproach.
Notes that Sita disregards both bodily hardship and the ignorant townsfolk's gossip, grounding her sacrifice in devotion.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of the three commentators (on 7.48.17)
commentaries.gist: All gloss her request that Lakshmana look at her as showing she is visibly pregnant, so there is a witness.
Sita's lament and message to Rama at the river (chapter read for context).

practical_reading: When falsely accused, it is natural to feel the injustice of the lie more than the hardship; naming that can help.
misreadings: Not a model of a wife accepting abandonment as right; our note is correct that she is the one wronged.
The 'husband is a woman's deity' line that follows must not be used to counsel submission to an unjust partner.
cautions: Context is a pregnant wife abandoned because of gossip; handle with care for readers facing separation, slut-shaming or community judgement.
Verse boundaries are tangled across editions.
speaks_to: someone hurt by rumours or false accusations
people judged by their community (caste, gossip, social media)
not_for: a reader being pressured to accept mistreatment from a spouse

verified_ref: Valmiki Ramayana 7.49.16-17 (Southern Recension, itihasa.io); Baroda critical edition 7.48.12-13. Our id 7.49.10 is six off.
attribution_note: Valmiki to Sita for the first verse; the second is the narrator describing Sita's reply. Our record lists only Valmiki.
translation_note: Accurate for the first verse ('idam arghyam' = this guest-offering, the formal welcome water). Our Sanskrit includes the next verse (Sita bows and says 'so be it', and follows the sage), which our translation leaves out.
context: Lakshmana has left Sita weeping alone at the Ganga. Valmiki, told by the hermit boys, comes with the guest-offering. He tells her he knows by his inner sight that she is sinless, that she is now under his care, that the women ascetics near his hermitage will look after her like their own child, and here: accept this welcome, trust me, let your fever of sorrow go, think of this as coming home. Sita bows at his feet, says 'so be it', and follows him; the sages' wives welcome her. Her twin sons Kusha and Lava are born there.

key_terms.sense: free of the fever of worry
as if arriving at your own home

core_teaching: Valmiki offers a wronged, abandoned woman belief, safety and a home: the first answer to rejection is welcome.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rāma Varmā's Tilaka and Govindarāja's Bhūṣaṇa
commentaries.gist: Complete the simile: dwell here just as in your own home; Tilaka glosses 'like a calf' in the previous verse as 'like one's own child'.
Calling Sita 'child' (vatse) reveals Valmiki's friendship with Janaka as well as Dasharatha.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of the three commentators (on 7.49.17-18)
commentaries.gist: Sita's quiet 'so be it', with bowed head and joined palms, shows dignity amid devastation; the sages' wives are the women ascetics he mentioned.
Has Valmiki come with the arghya, tell Sita he knows her purity by his spiritual vision, and assure her she is under his protection.

practical_reading: When someone arrives at your door rejected or shamed, believe them, make them safe, and let them feel at home.
misreadings: Not a suggestion that the abandonment was fine because she found shelter.
cautions: Two verses with different speakers merged.
speaks_to: someone starting over after being cast out (divorce, family rejection, displacement)
volunteers, hosts, shelter workers, teachers welcoming newcomers
not_for: a reader who has nowhere to go (could feel like a fairy-tale rescue)

verified_ref: Valmiki Ramayana 7.53.4 (Southern Recension, itihasa.io). Not in the Baroda critical edition (7.53 is an Appendix I / starred passage there).
translation_note: Accurate. 'Tan me marmāṇi kṛntati' = that cuts at my vitals.
context: After Sita's banishment, Rama has grieved and not held court for four days. Lakshmana has just consoled him, and Rama, pleased, calls him a rare kinsman. Here he says four days without attending to the citizens' business cuts him to the core; he orders the subjects, priest, ministers and all men and women with petitions summoned, adding that a king who does not attend to his people's affairs daily falls into a dreadful hell. He then tells the story of King Nriga, cursed for keeping petitioners waiting.

key_terms.sense: it cuts me to the core

core_teaching: Even in private grief, Rama feels his neglect of people who depend on him as a wound, and returns to duty.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rāma Varmā's Tilaka and Śivasahāya's Śiromaṇi
commentaries.gist: Supply 'have passed' to the elliptical opening; Śiromaṇi joins verses 4 and 5 as one sentence: the lapse torments Rama, so he summons everyone to fulfil their petitions at once.
Has Rama say four days have passed since he attended to his people's interests and his soul is tormented, then summon the petitioners.

practical_reading: Grief can take us away from responsibilities; when ready, return to them without self-punishment, starting with whoever has been waiting.
misreadings: Not a demand to suppress grief and get back to work immediately; Rama took four days.
The 'king falls into hell' line that follows is about rulers' duty, not a threat to grieving readers.
cautions: The grief here follows Rama's own unjust abandonment of Sita; a reading must not present him simply as the sufferer.
Southern-only passage.
speaks_to: someone returning to work or caregiving after a personal crisis
leaders and public servants who have let things slide
not_for: someone in fresh grief being pushed back to work too soon

verified_ref: Valmiki Ramayana 7.72.12 (Southern Recension, itihasa.io); Baroda critical edition 7.63.8. Our id 7.72.10 is two off.
translation_note: Accurate. 'Na ciraṃ pravasāmy aham' = I cannot stay away (abroad) any longer.
context: Shatrughna, sent by Rama to kill the demon Lavana, has founded and ruled the city of Madhura (Mathura) for twelve years. On a visit home he reports that all is done, says twelve years apart from Rama have been too long, and asks not to be sent away again: like a calf without its mother, he cannot live far away any longer. Rama embraces him, tells him not to lose heart since a king must protect his people, invites him to visit from time to time, and asks him to stay seven nights before returning.

key_terms.sense: like a calf without its mother
I cannot live away any longer

core_teaching: Shatrughna voices raw homesickness and longing for his brother after long service far away.

commentaries.gist: Glosses the plea as 'grant my request to stay with you', likening long absence from Rama to a calf separated from its mother.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Śiromaṇi and Govindarāja's Bhūṣaṇa (on 7.72.11)
commentaries.gist: Twelve full years have elapsed; with duty done, Shatrughna's pent-up longing breaks out, and the commentators let its simplicity speak.
Has Shatrughna report Lavana's death, say twelve years far from Rama are enough, and ask not to remain away like a calf separated from its mother.

practical_reading: Gives voice to homesickness after long service far from family; it is not weakness to say you miss home.
misreadings: Not childishness; the same verse reports a hard task completed.
speaks_to: migrants, soldiers, students, workers posted far from family
adult children missing parents or siblings
not_for: someone grieving a parent's death (the 'motherless calf' image may be too raw)
research_note: Our prasang field is empty; this pairs naturally with 7.72.14 as a 'longing and duty' prasang.

verified_ref: Valmiki Ramayana 7.72.16-17 (Southern Recension, itihasa.io); Baroda critical edition 7.63.12-13. Our id 7.72.14 is two off; itihasa 7.72.14 is Rama's line 'kings do not lose heart living far away; subjects must be protected'.
translation_note: Accurate. Our 'line' drops the duty half ('a kingdom must be looked after... then go back'); the verse insists he return. Śiromaṇi reads 'saptarātraṃ mayā saha' (seven nights with me), as in our Sanskrit.
context: Shatrughna has begged to stay near Rama after twelve years ruling Madhura. Rama embraces him, tells him not to despond, since kings do not lose heart abroad and must protect their subjects; he may visit from time to time. Here Rama says Shatrughna is dearer to him than life, but the kingdom must be looked after; so stay seven nights, then return with your people. Shatrughna, in a subdued voice, agrees, stays seven nights and goes back.
core_teaching: Rama holds love and duty together: he affirms his brother is dearer than life, gives him time together, and still sends him back to his responsibility.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rāma Varmā's Tilaka and Śivasahāya's Śiromaṇi (on 7.72.15-16)
commentaries.gist: Rama softens stern duty with warmth, inviting regular visits; Śiromaṇi notes his balanced candour: Shatrughna is beloved beyond life, yet the realm's protection cannot be neglected.
Because protecting Mathura cannot be set aside, Rama grants a seven-night reunion; Shatrughna's subdued 'so be it' shows him putting longing under dharma.
Has Rama say he too cherishes Shatrughna more than life, yet the kingdom's security comes first; stay seven days, then return to Madhura.

practical_reading: Love does not cancel duty: make time to be together fully, then return to your responsibilities, and plan the next visit.
misreadings: Not coldness: Rama embraces him and affirms his love first.
cautions: The response to homesickness is 'go back'; for a lonely reader that can feel hard. Pair with the invitation to visit (7.72.15).
speaks_to: parents and adult children who live apart
families saying goodbye at the end of a visit
people whose work keeps them far from loved ones
not_for: someone wanting permission to come home for good

verified_ref: Valmiki Ramayana 7.83.20 (Southern Recension, itihasa.io; a three-line verse); Baroda critical edition 7.74.19 (the first two lines are marked as southern additions in itihasa's text). Our id 7.83.15 is five off.
translation_note: Accurate. 'Lakṣmaṇapūrvaja' = elder brother of Lakshmana (Bharata). 'Bālānāṃ tu' is glossed by Tilaka and Śiromaṇi as 'even from the young'.
context: Having finished other duties, Rama proposes to perform the Rajasuya, the imperial sacrifice. Bharata gently objects that it would bring the destruction of many royal lines and suffering on earth, and Rama, the protector of all, should not do it. Rama is pleased, praises Bharata's words as firm and righteous, and gives up the plan: the wise should not do what afflicts the world, and good advice should be accepted even from the young. Lakshmana then proposes the Ashvamedha instead.

key_terms.sense: an act that brings suffering to the world
good words even from the young

core_teaching: A wise leader drops a plan that would harm people, and accepts good counsel even from a younger person.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rāma Varmā's Tilaka and Śivasahāya's Śiromaṇi
commentaries.gist: Both read 'bālānāṃ tu' as 'even from the young'; by accepting Bharata's correction, Rama shows the humility of a dharmic ruler, opening the way for the non-violent Ashvamedha proposal.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of the three commentators (on 7.83.19)
commentaries.gist: All unpack the compound for the Rajasuya that was 'about to enter my resolve'; Tilaka and Śiromaṇi supply that Rama turns back his intention.
Has Rama renounce the Rajasuya on Bharata's counsel, say the wise should never do what harms the world, and that good advice should be taken even from a child.

practical_reading: Be willing to drop your own grand plan when someone, even someone junior, shows it would hurt people.
misreadings: Not that elders are always wrong; the point is openness to good counsel from any quarter.
speaks_to: managers, parents and teachers receiving feedback from juniors or children
leaders weighing projects with human costs
not_for: a reader needing comfort rather than guidance

verified_ref: Valmiki Ramayana 7.97.3ef-4 (Southern Recension, itihasa.io); Baroda critical edition 7.88.3 (a three-line verse there). Reference essentially correct.
attribution_note: Rama to Valmiki (before the assembly), correct.
translation_note: Accurate. 'Tad bhavān kṣantum arhati' = 'so you, sir, should forgive (me)', addressed to Valmiki, not to Sita; our 'Please forgive me' is right but a reader may assume he asks Sita. Śiromaṇi reads 'lokabhayāt' as fear of (scriptural) censure.
context: Years after the banishment, Valmiki brings Sita to Rama's assembly during the Ashvamedha and swears to her purity. Rama answers with joined palms: he accepts Valmiki's word; Sita proved herself before the gods long ago, yet public slander was powerful, and knowing she was innocent he abandoned her out of fear of the people; he asks Valmiki's forgiveness, acknowledges Kusha and Lava as his sons, and wants Sita proven pure before the world. Sita instead calls on the Earth, which rises and takes her; she does not return.

key_terms.sense: knowing full well she was sinless
out of fear of the people

core_teaching: Rama admits he abandoned Sita knowing she was innocent, because he feared public opinion, and asks pardon; the confession does not undo the wrong, and Sita refuses another trial.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rāma Varmā's Tilaka
commentaries.gist: Clears Rama of private suspicion: knowing Sita sinless, he banished her purely from fear of public talk; he consents to a fresh proof only to silence that slander.
Reads 'fear of the people' as dread of scriptural censure, and says Rama begs Valmiki's pardon for the offence of the abandonment.
Rama's 'so it is' means the proof must be done not for his own trust, which Valmiki's oath already gave, but for the public.
Has Rama say that though convinced of her innocence, he cast off Sita from fear of the people, ask the brahmin's pardon, and acknowledge the twins.

practical_reading: Admitting a wrong done under social pressure is necessary but does not by itself repair it; giving in to what people say can cost the people we love most.
misreadings: As our note says: the admission does not undo the wrong.
Not a defence of putting reputation over justice; the commentators' attempts to excuse Rama should not be presented as the verse's meaning.
cautions: Leads directly to Sita leaving for the earth; for readers who were disbelieved or abandoned it may be painful.
Commentators largely defend Rama; a reading should not force that frame on a hurting reader.
speaks_to: someone who gave in to family or community pressure and hurt an innocent person
people facing honour or reputation pressures
the person wronged who hears an apology that comes too late
not_for: a reader being pressured to accept an apology and reconcile
